text:
Verses 10-25

(7:10) Certainly We have established you in the earth, and made in it [various] means of livelihood for you. Little do you thank.

(7:11) Certainly We created you, then We formed you, then We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam.” So they [all] prostrated, but not Iblīs: he was not among those who prostrated.

(7:12) Said He, “What prevented you from prostrating, when I commanded you?” “I am better than him,” he said. “You created me

from fire and You created him from clay.”

(7:13) “Get down from it!” He said. “It is not for you to be arrogant therein. Begone! You are indeed among the degraded ones.”

(7:14) He said, “Respite me till the day they will be resurrected.”

(7:15) Said He, “You are indeed among the reprieved.”

(7:16) “As You have consigned me to perversity,” he said, “I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path.

(7:17) Then I will come at them from their front and from their rear, and from their right and their lef , and You will not find most of them to be grateful.”

(7:18) Said He, “Begone hence, blameful, banished! Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill hell with you all.”

(7:19) [Then He said to Adam,] “O Adam, dwell with your mate in paradise, and eat thereof whence you wish; but do not approach this tree, lest you should be among the wrongdoers.”

(7:20) Then Satan tempted them, to expose to them what was hidden from them of their shameful parts, and he said, “Your Lord has only forbidden you from this tree lest you should become angels, or lest you become immortal.”

(7:21) And he swore to them, “I am indeed your well-wisher.”

(7:22) Thus he brought about their fall by deception. So when they tasted of the tree, their shameful parts became exposed to them, and they began to stitch over themselves with the leaves of paradise. Their Lord called out to them, “Did I not forbid you from

that tree, and tell you that Satan is indeed your manifest enemy?”

(7:23) They said, “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves! If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

(7:24) He said, “Get down, being enemies of one another! On the earth shall be your abode and sustenance for some time.”

(7:25) He said, “In it you will live, and in it you will die; and from it you will be raised [from the dead].”

Introduction

These verses discuss the creation of humankind, God’s command to the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam, and their abidance. They also discuss Satan’s defiance, his deception of Adam and his wife, their expulsion from the garden, and God’s decrees with respect to these events.

Commentary

(7:10) Certainly We have established you (makkanākum, from tamkīn) in the earth, and made in it [various] means of livelihood (maʿāyish) for you. Little do you thank.

Tamkīn is synonymous with iskān and īṭān (to give someone residence, to establish someone in a place, to make someone settle somewhere). The meaning is: “We have made the earth your place (makān).” Another possible meaning for tamkīn is “to give someone power and authority in some

territory.” This meaning can be confirmed by making a parallel between the current set of verses and a similar account of the story of Adam and Satan in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the story is preceded by reference to humankind’s God-given power and authority in creation: It is He who created for you all that is in the earth (2:29).

However, the first meaning is more consonant with what we read below at the end of this story: On the earth shall be your abode and sustenance for some time (7:24). We can say that what we read in the current

verse—Certainly We have established you in the earth (7:10)—is a brief description, which is then elaborated in the subsequent verses, until the end of the story of Adam’s garden [in verse 7:25].

Maʿāyish is the plural of maʿīshah, which means “an instrument or means of living” such as food, drink and so on. The verse’s tone and theme is to show two of God’s favors upon humankind: (1) giving them dwelling on the earth (or giving them power and authority in it); and (2) providing them with various means of livelihood. That is why the verse ends by

saying: Little do you thank.

(7:11) Certainly (la-qad) We created you, then We formed you, then We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam.” So they [all] prostrated, but not Iblīs: he was not among those who prostrated.

The story of Adam starts here, until verse 25. These verses expound on the concise version of humankind’s creation mentioned in the last verse, and explain how humankind ended up being established in the earth, as we read: Certainly We have established you in the earth, and made in it [various] means of livelihood(7:10). That is why the verse starts with the letter

lām, indicating a vow for emphasis (called lām al-qasam).1 Likewise, the two stories mentioned in these verses—that is, the story of commanding the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam, and the story of Adam’s garden—are presented in a single thread, as opposed to being separated into two accounts. Otherwise, the two stories are really independent of one another, but they are merged together because this way the brief introduction mentioned in the last verse—Certainly We have established you in the earth… (7:10)—matches the conclusion of the two stories joined together: He said, “Get down, being enemies of one another! On the earth shall be your abode…” (7:24-25).

Certainly We created you, then We formed you…: This verse is addressed to all humankind, with a tone of describing God’s favor upon them, just like the last verse. The two verses pursue the same theme, with the difference that the current verse elaborates on the concise account of the last. Hence, the verse begins with a universal address to all humankind: Certainly We created you, then We formed you, but then it switches

to a particular statement about Adam as a specific person: then We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam.” We can infer two points from this transition:

(i) The prostration of the angels was in fact directed toward all humankind as children of Adam. Adam was set up as a qiblah (direction) for their

prostration. He was a representative of the entire human race, presented to the angels on behalf of all humans. He was much like the Kaʿbah, which is

1 The connection is that the letter lām (lit. certainly, indeed) conveys a sense of justification and explanation. In other words, it shows that what follows next is an explanation for what was mentioned before. (Trans.)

set as a qiblah. Facing the Kaʿbah in worship symbolizes facing the Lord. Therefore, their prostration was not made to Adam as a specific individual. There are three Qur’anic proofs for this idea—that Adam is a representative of all humankind in the story of the prostration: (1) Verses 2:30-33,

where the angels are commanded to prostrate before Adam because of his position of khilāfah (successorship, vicegerency). The khilāfah mentioned there [in verse 2:30] is not something exclusive to Adam, but it is common to all humankind, as we explained under the verses. Therefore, the

consequent prostration would also pertain to all humankind. (2) Below we read that Satan (Iblīs) says: As You have consigned me to perversity I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will come at them from their front and from their rear… (7:16-17). In these verses, the plural pronouns refer to all humans, without the intermediation of Adam, and without any explicit reference to humankind in the previous verses. A similar reference to them [through plural pronouns] is found in Sūrah al-Ḥijr, where Satan says: My Lord! As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely glamorize [evil] for them on the earth, and I will surely

pervert them all (15:39). Likewise, in Sūrah Ṣād he says: By Your might, I will surely pervert them all (38:82). Clearly if the prostration of the angels were not made to all humankind, it would not make sense for Satan to demonstrate such outright hostility against them all. (3) God addresses Adam [and Eve] in Sūrah al-Baqarah and Sūrah Ṭā-Hā [verses 2:38 and 20:123], while He makes the same address to the children of Adam in the current chapter, where He says: O Children of Adam! If there come to you messengers from among yourselves (7:35).1 (ii) The creation of Adam is tantamount to the creation of all humankind. This can also be inferred from the following verses: And He commenced the creation of man from clay. Then He made his progeny from an

extract of a base fluid (32:7-8); It is He who created you from dust, then from a drop of [seminal] fluid, then from a clinging mass (40:67). These verses suggest that creation from dust pertains to the creation of Adam [while his descendants were not directly created from dust]. This point can also be deduced from another account of this story in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ,

1 Verse 20:123 starts with a dual pronoun—corresponding to Adam and Eve— but it continues with a plural pronoun. Verse 2:38 also uses a plural pronoun. Given verse 7:35, these plural pronouns most likely refer to all humankind (that is, Adam, Eve and their progeny). (Trans.)

where Satan says to God: If You respite me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely harness his [Adam’s] progeny, [all] except a few (17:62). There is also some allusion to this point where God says: When your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them bear witness over themselves… (7:172ff), as we shall discuss below. Other exegetes have offered a variety of interpretations for this verse. Majmaʿ al-bayān says: “God continues in this verse to describe His blessings [upon His servants] at the beginning of [their] creation: Certainly

We created you, then (thumma) We formed you (7:11).” Then it provides a list of interpretations for the word thumma (lit. then) in this verse: (1) According to al-Akhfash, the word thumma is synonymous with the letter wāw (lit. and) in this verse.

(2) Al-Zajjāj has objected to al-Akhfash by saying that this is a mistake that is not permitted by al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and all reliable

scholars [of Arabic grammar]. Instead, thumma is exclusively used to introduce an event that occurs after what is mentioned before the term.1 W hat is meant in this verse is: “We first created Adam, and then We fashioned him.” In other words, God began the creation of Adam from dust, and then applied a form to it afterwards. This is the meaning of We created you, then We formed you. Once Adam was created, then We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam” (7:11). This interpretation is narrated from al-Ḥasan [al-Baṣrī]. It is common among Arabs to say, “We did this to you”

when what they mean is, “We did this to your fathers.” Likewise we read in the Qur’an [addressing the Jews]: And when We took a pledge from you, and raised the Mount above you (2:63), which means, “We took a pledge from your ancestors.”

(3) The verse means: “We created Adam, then We formed you in his loins, then We told the angels: Prostrate to Adam.” This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and al-Suddī.

(4) The sequence in the verse [inferred from the word thumma (then)] pertains to the sequence of God’s report of the events [not the occurrence of the events]. The meaning is: “We created you, then We formed you, then We inform you that We said to

1 In other words, thumma marks a temporal separation between what is mentioned before and after it. (Trans.)

the angels: Prostrate before Adam.”1 This is like when someone says, “I am walking, then (thumma) I am speeding.”2 This is how several scholars of [Arabic] grammar have interpreted the verse, such as ʿAlī b. ʿĪsá, Qāḍī Abū Saʿīd al-Sīrāfī and others.

(5) Following the same notion [that thumma sometimes indicates a sequence of expression, not a sequence of occurrence], some exegetes have interpreted the verse as follows: “We created you in the loins of men, and (thumma)3 We formed you in the wombs of women.” This is narrated from ʿIkrimah.

(6) Another similar interpretation is: “We created you in the wombs, and (thumma) We formed you by opening ears, eyes and other organs [for you].”

(End of quote from Majmaʿ al-bayān.)

There are two problems with the interpretation narrated from al-Zajjāj [number 2]:

(1) In order to attribute the acts of fathers to their children, there must be some common quality between the two groups to validate the attribution. A mere blood tie is not sufficient for merging the two groups in one

category. The fact that all humans are the descendants of Adam does not suffice to count Adam’s creation as theirs. Instead, their creation must be somehow incorporated in Adam’s.

(2) Granted that the creation and formation of Adam counts as the creation and formation of his descendants, it follows that commanding the angels to prostrate to Adam is equivalent to commanding them to prostrate to his descendants. Therefore, the verse should have been similar to the verse: And when We took a pledge from you, and raised the Mount above you (2:63). However, the verse does not tel the angles, “Prostrate before humans,” but it says: “Prostrate before Adam” (7:11).

1 According to this interpretation, only the second thumma pertains to God’s report of the event, but the first thumma pertains to the occurrence of the event. (Trans.)

2 In expressions like this, thumma means “rather.” The meaning is: “I am walking; rather I am speeding.” It could also mean “and”: “I am walking and speeding.” Put simply: “I am walking fast.” (Trans.)

3 In this interpretation, and the next one, thumma can also mean “then,” indicating the temporal sequence of events, which is the most apparent and primary meaning of the term. (Trans.)

As with the interpretations narrated after that, they are all weak possibilities without any textual evidence from the verse. Those who have

offered these views would certainly not consent to their own speech being interpreted as such, so how come they have interpreted the most eloquent speech in this way?!

… So they [all] prostrated, but not Iblīs: he was not among those who prostrated: All angels prostrated, which is mentioned explicitly in the verse: Thereat the angels prostrated, all of them together (15:30). The verse excludes Iblīs (Satan, the Devil) from the list. God explains the reason for his noncompliance elsewhere: He [Iblīs] was one of the jinn, so

he transgressed against his Lord’s command (18:50). However, concerning the angels God says: Rather, they are [His] honoured servants. They do not venture to speak ahead of Him, and they act by His command (21:26-27). These verses clearly show that Iblīs was not of the same kind as the angels. This has led to a controversy among the scholars. Some have suggested that the command to the angels also included Iblīs, but only the

angels are mentioned based on generalization (taghlīb),1 since the angels were greater in number and higher in status. This way, we can maintain the exception in the verse as a connected exception.2 Others have suggested that Iblīs was commanded separately, meaning that God made two

commands: one to the angels, and one to Iblīs, even though the following verse suggests that God made only one command. He holds Iblīs accountable for the same command addressed to the angels: What prevented you

from prostrating, when I commanded you? (7:12). Given this interpretation [that there were two commands], the exception in the verse would be an unconnected exception.

Based on Qur’anic evidence, we can say that Iblīs was with the angels, without any distinction between them. They were all united in the station of quds (sanctity), as it can be inferred from the story of [Adam’s] khilāfah (successorship, vicegerency) in the Qur’an: When your Lord said to the

1 Taghlīb is when a mixed group is entirely described by the quality of some of them, even though that quality does not apply to all of them. (Trans.)

2 A “connected exception” (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) is an ordinary exception, where what is excepted is a member of the original group. Its opposite is “unconnected exception” (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, istithnāʾ munfaṣil), where what is excepted is not a member of the original group. Such exception effectively conveys two independent statements. (Trans.)

angels, “Indeed I am going to set a viceroy on the earth,” they said, “Will You set in it someone who will cause corruption in it, and shed blood, while we celebrate Your praise and proclaim Your sanctity?”(2:30). The command to prostrate before Adam was directed at that station, including anyone positioned in it. Therefore the audience of the command included anyone at that level, based on the position that they held. There is some reference to this station in what we shall read below, where God says to Iblīs: “Get down from it! It is not for you to be arrogant therein” (7:13). The pronouns “it” and “therein” refer to either his position (manzilah), or the celestial realm (samāʾ), or the garden [of Adam]—which all reduce to his spiritual station and status. If the command were made to the audience [that is, the angels and Iblīs] irrespective of their station, the verse should have said, “It is not for you to be arrogant” [without qualifying it by “therein”]. Given the above explanations, there was no difference between Iblīs and the angels before the command to prostrate to Adam, but afterwards they divided into two groups. On the one hand, there were the angels who persisted with the same station and position that they had, which consisted of humble servitude before the Truth and obedience to God’s command. This defines the reality of the angels’ life and the kind of acts they perform, as God describes them: Rather, they are [His] honoured servants.

They do not venture to speak ahead of Him, and they act by His command

(21:26-27). On the other hand, there was Iblīs, who lefiithe station that he previously shared with the angels. God says: He [Iblīs] was one of the jinn, so he transgressed (fa-fasaqa, from fisq) against his Lord’s command

(18:50). The original usage of the word fisq is when a date comes out of its sheath. In like manner, an essential property of the path chosen by Iblīs was coming out of his divine position of servitude and obedience. He differentiated himself from the angels by opting for such a life.

The Qur’an has depicted this story in a way that mimics a human interaction between a ruler and his subjects. It talks about things like command, compliance, defiance, argument, expulsion and eviction. However,

based on our explanation above and the verses that we quoted, we can see that these are symbolic expressions for a transcendent reality in the world of creation. What is meant is that Iblīs (Satan, the Devil) did not comply to humble himself before the reality and essence of humankind. This was a disobedience on his part, given the [spiritual and existential] station that he had. We can deduce this from God’s address to him: It is not for you to be arrogant therein (7:13). In other words, it was fundamentally incompatible with his station [indicated by “therein” in verse 7:13]

to be arrogant. Hence, his arrogance was tantamount to exiting that level and falling to abyss.

We also explained that there was only a single command which was addressed to both the angels and Iblīs [on the account of their common station]. However, the angels are created in a way that their existence is fixed on obedience and good. This means that they do not face the option to obey or disobey. These two choices are not equally open to them, which means that they are not subject to legislative (tashrīʿī) and authoritative (mawlawī) commands. From this we can infer a similar, but opposite, point about the creation and existence of Iblīs: his essence is characterized by disobedience.

Had it not been for God’s creation of Adam, and His command to the angels and Iblīs to prostrate before him, Iblīs would have remained in his station of divine proximity without any distinction from the angels. However, the creation of Adam split that station into two: the station of proximity [to God], versus the station of distance [from God]. Thus it resulted in two paths: the path of happiness, and the path of wretchedness.

(7:12) Said He, “What prevented you (manaʿaka, from man.) from (an-lā) prostrating, when I commanded you?” “I am better than him,” he said. “You created me from fire and You created him from clay.”

In Sūrah Ṣād we read: He said, “O Iblīs! What keeps you from prostrating before that which I have created with My [own] two hands?” (38:75),

where the verse does not include the negative particle lā after the particle an. That is why some exegetes have said that the negative particle lā is is zāʾidah (extra, redundant, semantically empty) in this verse, added only for emphasis. Hence, the meaning is: “W hat prevented you from prostrating?”1 Another example of an extra lā is the verse: So that the People of the

1 If we include the negative particle lā in the meaning, the verse would be saying: “What prevented you from not prostrating?” which is clearly not the intended meaning in the verse, especially given verse 38:75. A similar extra lā is found in verses 20:92-93. (Trans.)

Book may (li-an-lā) know that they have no power over anything of Allah’s grace (57:29).1 However, it is more appropriate to say that the negative lā indicates an implied omitted verb—like ḥaml (to make someone do something) or daʿá (to provoke)—which is implicitly included in the verb manʿ (to prevent). The meaning would be: “What was the stumbling block which made you—or instigated you—to not prostrate?”

… “I am better than him,” he said. “You created me from fire and You created him from clay.”: This is the answer of the cursed Satan to God. It expresses his first sin; rather, the first disobedience of God. All other sins can be analyzed and reduced to a similar claim of egoism and conceit, where one assumes some greatness for oneself before the grandeur of God. However, all greatness belongs to Him, and He has no partner in that. Since everything is humbled before God; the entire world of existence is subservient to Him; all heads bow down in submission to Him; and all voices are calmed before Him—a servant that is created by God is in no position to say “I” before God’s existence.

Satan’s problem was that he looked only at himself and saw his being alone, as an independent entity. He failed to look up and see the Lord Who is standing above him, and Who keeps him [and all beings] on their feet. Had he done that, his sense of self ood and ego would have dissolved completely, such that he would no longer feel any greatness or independent existence in himself. Then, with his soul humbled, he would have submitted to God and obeyed His command willingly. In that case, instead of seeing himself as better than Adam because of being created of fire as opposed to clay, he would only concern himself with the command that had been issued from the source and origin of all beauty, majesty, magnificence and grandeur.

From a grammatical point of view, if Satan’s answer were to be commensurate with God’s question—What prevented you from prostrating,

when I commanded you—he should have said: “What prevented me was that I am better than him (manaʿanī annī khayr minhu).” But instead he said: I am better than him. This subtle difference highlights Satan’s sense of ego, and also shows that this was something established and persistent in him.2 This is an important point, because it shows that Satan’s arrogance

1 Translated literally (including the negative particle lā) the verse would mean: “So that the People of the Book may not know…” (Trans.)

2 Manaʿanī annī khayr minhu is a verbal sentence (fiʿliyyah) which proves only was against God, not against Adam.

Given Satan’s answer, what prevented him from prostration was his impression of being “better”: I am better than him. Nothing shows arrogance more clearly and strongly than saying that “I am better.”

The sentence,“I am better than him,” he said. “You created me from fire and You created him from clay”shows that Satan’s proof for being better than Adam was that he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. God says in the Qur’an that Satan was one of the jinn: He [Iblīs] was one of the jinn, so he transgressed against his Lord’s command (18:50); and the jinn were created from fire: Certainly We created man out of a dry clay [drawn] from an aging mud, and We created the jinn earlier out of a piercing fire (15:26-27); He created man out of dry clay, like the potter’s, and created the jinn out of a flame of a fire (55:14-15). Therefore, God confirms that Satan was created from fire. However, God does not confirm Satan’s claim to superiority over Adam. He does not reject this claim here, but the story of khilāfah (successorship, vicegerency) in Sūrah al-Baqarah [verses 2:30ff] clearly show the merit of Adam over Satan and the angels. The same story is mentioned elsewhere as follows: When your Lord said to the angels, “Indeed I am about to create a human being out of clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down in prostration before him.” Thereat the angels prostrated, all of them together, but not Iblīs; he acted arrogantly and he was one of the faithless. He said, “O Iblīs! What keeps you from prostrating before that which I

have created with My [own] two hands? Are you arrogant, or are you [one] of the exalted ones?” “I am better than him,” he said. “You created me from fire and You created him from clay” (38:71-76). These verses show that the angels were not ordered to prostrate to Adam due to his earthly and material creation. Rather, they were told to prostrate to him after he was proportioned and received the divine spirit. “My spirit” here is an honorific ascription to the divine; it shows that the human spirit has a unique status and a very special position in the sight of God. In the world of creation, nothing has any merit of its own, but it is only one’s position with respect to God which determines who is better.

a single occurrence of the verb (“to prevent”) in the past. However, I am better than him is a nominal sentence (ismiyyah) without a verb in Arabic. Thus it indicates that the predicate (“am better than him”) is established for the subject across time. (Trans.)

In addition, God reprimands Iblīs by asking him: What keeps you from prostrating before that which I have created with My [own] two hands?

(38:75). Using one’s “both hands” to create something show’s the Maker’s utmost degree of attention and regard for that thing—irrespective of how we interpret the “two hands” of God. This is, in turn, a merit for Adam. In response to this question, however, Satan ignored his arrogance against God, and only referred to their initial substance of fire and clay: I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay (38:

76). Similarly, in the current chapter God asks him: What prevented you from prostrating, when I commanded you? This question shows that Satan’s problem was being arrogant against his Lord [not against Adam], since he did not comply with God’s command. But again, we see that he pays no attention to explaining the reason behind his arrogance against God, as he only says: I am better than him…

This sentence—I am better than him—is in a sense related to Satan’s arrogance against God, because it implies a claim to an independent existence for him against God’s absolute existence which overshadows all beings. This sense of independence was what led Satan to forget God’s grandeur, and instead assume a similar position for himself irrespective of his Lord. It was incumbent on him to obey God because He is God, but Satan overlooked this reality due to viewing himself as an independent entity. As a result, he assessed the two options available to him, and

decided that disobedience is better than obedience, that transgression is preferred to submission. The root cause of all this was his proud assumption of some independence in existence for himself. That blinded him

from seeing the truth, and led him to reason [for himself] that his origin of fire is better than Adam’s origin of clay, and it is not right for the superior to humble himself before the inferior through prostration, even if

God commands him to do so. Satan ignored God’s command because he saw himself equal to God and parallel to Him in terms of independence and greatness. Thus he overlooked the Commander and decided to assess the two sides of the command.

The point is that God is the Origin and End of all things. His command is either His very act of creation, or it reduces to His creation and

existentiation (takwīn). Therefore, if He creates something and decrees some merit for it, then that thing will have the merit in reality and the fact of the matter. Likewise, if He creates something and orders it to humble itself before the first being, it means that the second being is less perfect than the first one in terms of existence.His word is the truth; and it is incumbent that His order is obeyed because it is His order, not because of any interest, benefit or consideration (maslahah) that it involves. Otherwise, God would be stripped of His lordship (rubūbiyyah) and authority (mawlawiyyah), and would make considerations of interests and benefits central to everything. Since those considerations and benefits pertain to His creatures, that would set God on par with the other things.1 Putting together all verses about this story, we can conclude that the root cause behind Stan’s sin was his arrogant defiance against God’s command, which qualified him for God’s curse [that is, his expulsion from his

station of divine proximity]. Satan expressed his pride by saying: I am better than him [Adam]. He deemed himself better than Adam, and viewed

Adam to be an abject being. However, Adam was chosen by God. God had notified the angels and Satan about Adam’s superiority over them in the story of khilāfah [verses 2:30ff], and also through expressions like: when I breathe into him of My spirit (38:72) and: I created him with My [own] two hands (38:75). Hence, Satan was certainly arrogant against Adam, but as we explained above, what underlay his behavior was arrogance against God. What is central to this story in the Qur’an is Satan’s pride against God, not his pride against Adam. We can see this in the verse: When We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” they prostrated, but not Iblīs. He was one of the jinn, so he transgressed against his Lord’s command (18:50). Note that the verse does not say, “He refused to humble himself before Adam” but it only refers to his transgression against God’s command.2 To summarize, the verses about this story are primarily concerned with Satan’s arrogant defiance against his Lord. His arrogance against

1 This is based on the view that God’s commands are not arbitrary or merely conventional (called iʿtibārī), but they are based on some reality in the world of

existence (called ḥaqīqī). Our laws are based on social contract and convention, while His laws are based on the relative position of different entities on the graded chain of existence. This is the reason why “it is incumbent that His order is obeyed because it is His order,” and also the reason why He is not questioned concerning what He does (21:23). That is because Allah is the Truth

(22:6, 22:62, 31:30); The truth is from your Lord (2:147, 3:60). (Trans.)

2 In other words, he transgressed against his Lord’s command (18:50) is used interchangeably for “he refused to prostrate.” This shows their equivalence. (Trans.)

Adam and his arguments to this effect are rather the consequences and implications of this root problem. This seems to be the reason why God does not give any direct answer to Satan’s justification [that I am better than him…]. There is only some allusion to this matter in certain verses, such as: when I breathe into him of My spirit (38:72) and: I created him with My [own] two hands (38:75).

Objection: According to the above interpretation, the command to prostrate before Adam was a takwīnī (existential, creational, causal) order. This, however, contradicts the idea of Satan’s “sin” and “disobedience” because disobedience is only applicable with respect to tashrīʿī (legislative, imperative) orders. God’s takwīnī command results in the inevitable

creation and occurrence of the event. If His takwīnī will is applied to any event, then it is impossible for it not to occur. He says: All that We say to a thing, when We will it, is to say to it “Be!” and it is (16:40).

Response: As we explained above, even though this story is expressed in a way that mimics common human interactions—including command, compliance, disobedience, expulsion and so on—it represents existential and creational realities that exist between humankind, the angels and the Devil. In other words, the story explains the creation and makeup of the angels and Satan, which have some relationship with humankind. It shows us the inherent inclinations of each side [the angels and Satan] with respect to human happiness and misery. This, however, does not mean that the command to prostrate before Adam was a takwīnī command.

This is the story of creation, expressed in a worldly picture, based on social interactions that we are accustomed to. It resembles a king who observes one of his subjects to have a special aptitude and capacity for growth, so he chooses him for himself, pays exclusive attention to him, makes him his vicegerent in his territory, and gives him priority over his courtiers. The king commands his courtiers to respect the special subject’s position and be in his service. Most of them respond positively to

this call and obey the king, which makes him pleased with them and lets them maintain their position. One of them, however, refuses to obey on the account that the king was wrong to make that directive. He argues that he is higher than the chosen subject in terms of inherent worth and record of service. As a result, the king is enraged by him, expels him from his court, and brands him with humiliation and dishonor. The reason is that [in a context of absolute monarchy,] a king is to obeyed because he is the central authority, the affairs are in his hands, and all commands issue from him, not because of his commands corresponding with some real benefit, interest or consideration. The latter corresponds to an advisor or counsellor whose job is to show others the way to [their] good and growth. In this analogy, the courtiers of the king—including those who obey his command and the one who does not—are all positioned at the same level of proximity, honor and presence, without any distinction between them. Then, after receiving the king’s command, their ways branch into two and they form two groups: (1) a group that is obedient and docile; and (2) a group that is disobedient and proud. The command also provides the grounds for the king to manifest his will, his power, and some

of his hidden qualities. As a result, he shows mercy to some, and wrath to others; he brings some near to himself, and expels others from himself; he pardons and forgives some, and captures and avenges others; he

encourages obedience with good promise, and discourages disobedience with threat; he rewards those who obey, and punishes those who disobey. Events like this can be compared to a touchstone that is applied to a metal to determine how genuine it is in reality.

The story of the angels’ prostration and Satan’s refusal represents certain realities that can be compared to the above picture. The command to

prostrate before Adam represents God’s honoring Adam with the station of divine proximity, divine khilāfah (successorship, vicegerency), and divine wilāyah (guardianship, authority, mastership). The angels submitted to this honorable position of Adam, while Iblīs turned away from it

because he was inherently opposed to human perfection and felicity. For this reason, whenever he comes in contact with humankind, he causes mischief for them; and whenever he approaches them, he leads them astray: About him [Satan] it has been decreed that should anyone take him for a friend, he will lead him astray (22:4).

God’s act of creation and giving existence (takwīn) is mentioned in several verses in the form of a verbal order or a similar form, such as: And He said to it [the heaven] and to the earth, “Come! Willingly or unwillingly!” They said, “We come willingly” (41:11); Indeed We presented the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it, and were apprehensive of it (33:72). This is expressed in the most comprehensive way in the verse: All His command, when He wills something, is to say

to it “Be,” and it is (36:82).

Objection: We cannot renounce the apparent form of the story and interpret it as merely pointing to some aspect of the creation [of Adam, Satan and the angels], because that would subject the Qur’an to ambiguity and subjective interpretations. If we sanction such interpretation in this story, then other teachings of the Qur’an—about God and the hereafter, as well as all Qur’anic stories, lessons and laws—may be taken to be figurative as well. That would completely destroy the religion.

Response: We follow wherever evidence takes us. In some cases we have evidence [from the Qur’an, sunnah and reason] that the apparent and literal meaning of the text is intended, as in the case of the principle beliefs, the primary teachings of the Qur’an, the stories of the past

prophets with their people, legal rulings, and their subsequent rewards and punishments. In some other cases, we have evidence against a literal meaning, such as the current story of discussion, as well as the realm of pre-existence (ʿālam al-dharr) [in verses 7:172-174] and the offering of divine covenant to the beings [in verse 33:72]. In these cases we can opt for a symbolic interpretation [referring to a reality about God’s creation] as long as it does not contravene an essential religious belief, a decisive verse, an authentic tradition (sunnah), or a proven rational argument. Satan’s argument for not prostrating to Adam was: I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay. This is a case of qiyās (reasoning by analogy, comparison), which is an argument not based on certainty, but based on probabilistic personal opinion. Such arguments are not strong enough to prove any fact. Exegetes have discussed

many points to show why his argument was fiawed, but as we explained above, the Qur’an does not address this issue. Instead, God reprimands him for showing arrogant defiance in a position that was only compatible with submission and compliance. That is why we will skip the discussions of the exegetes in this regard.

(7:13) “Get down from it!” He said. “It is not for you to be arrogant (tatakabbara, from takabbur) therein. Begone! You are indeed among the degraded ones (al-ṭāghirīn).”

Takabbur means “assuming greatness for oneself and expressing it to someone else.” Kibar (greatness, bigness, grandeur) and ṣighar (smallness, littleness, insignificance) are relative qualities which are usually used for non-physical matters. If one says or does something which implies that he is better and more important than another person, then he is counting himself great and the other side small. This is called takabbur. If any

being has any advantage or significance with respect to another being, it is through a quality that is due to God and from Him. This means that no one is entitled to express greatness of oneself (takabbur) except God. Hence, this is one of the exclusive attributes of God, Who is absolutely Great and Superior [to the entire existence]. Therefore, we can classify two types of takabbur (arrogance, pride): (1) rightful and praiseworthy pride, which belongs to God or traces to Him in some way, such as acting proudly against the enemies of God, for that is in reality seeking superiority from God; (2) wrong and blameworthy pride, which is found among others, where they claim some baseless greatness and significance for themselves. Ṣāghirīn is the plural of ṣāghir (abased, degraded, humiliated), which is derived from ṣaghār, meaning “abasement and dishonor.” Ṣaghār is like ṣighar (smallness, littleness, insignificance), except that the former is used as a non-physical attribute, while the latter is used as a physical property. The humiliation mentioned here was Satan’s penalty for being arrogant. The last statement in the verse—Begone! You are indeed among the degraded ones—interprets and emphasizes the first sentence: Get down (fa-ihbiṭ, from hubūṭ) from it. Hubūṭ means “to descend and go down from one’s position.” Therefore, Satan’s hubūṭ (descent, relegation) was not a physical movement from one location to another, but it was a spiritual descent to a lower status. This confirms what we said previously—that the pronouns “from it” and “therein” refer to Satan’s position of divine proximity, not the heavens or the garden, unless the heavens and the garden

are also meant in a spiritual sense.

The meaning is: God said to Satan, “Get down from your station because you did not prostrate when I ordered you. This is a station of humbleness and submission to Me. You are in no position to show pride here. Thus, you must leave, for indeed you are among those who are degraded and abased.”

(7:14-15) He said, “Respite me till the day they will be resurrected.” Said He, “You are indeed among the reprieved.”

Here Satan asks for a deferral [of his judgment and punishment], and God gives him respite. The Qur’an has discussed this more elaborately elsewhere: He said, “My Lord! Respite me till the day they will be resurrected.” Said He, “You are indeed among the reprieved until the day of the

known time” (38:79-81). These verses show that God did not grant Satan’s wish in the unconditional way that he requested. He did not respite Satan until the Day of Resurrection, but appointed a term before then, called “the day of the known time.” We shall discuss this, by the will of God, in

Sūrah al-Ḥijr [under verses 15:36-38].

Satan asked for his term to be extended until the Day of Resurrection, which means that he wanted to be able to deceive and tempt humankind throughout their existence in this world and the barzakh (the intermediate realm between this life and the Resurrection). However, God did

not grant his wish all the way to the Resurrection. Instead, He only gave Satan freedom to operate until the end of this life, but not during the barzakh. Hence, Satan cannot deceive and tempt the people after their death,

although he may be with some people in the realms after this world as a mate and companion, as we can infer from these verses: Whoever turns a blind eye to the remembrance of the All-Merciful, We assign him a devil who remains his companion. Indeed they bar them from the way while they suppose that they are [rightly] guided. When he comes to Us, he will say, “I wish there had been between me and you the distance between east and west! What an evil companion [you are]!” “Today that will be of no avail to you. As you did wrong, so will you share in the punishment” (43:36-39). This is also what is apparently meant [by “mates”] in the verse: Muster the wrongdoers and their mates and what they used to worship (37:22).

(7:16-17)“As You (fa-bi-mā) have consigned me to perversity (aghwaytanī, from ighwā.),” he said, “I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will come at them from their front and from their rear, and from their right and their lef , and You will not find most of them to be grateful.”

Ighwāʾ is to “cast someone into ghayy,” where ghayy (which is synonymous with ghawāyah) means “error, loss, failure and destruction.” Exegetes have suggested all of these meanings for ghayy in Satan’s

statement: As You have consigned me to perversity. However, what is meant here by ghayy is the first meaning [that is, error], based on a similar verse in Sūrah al-Ḥijr: He [Satan] said, “My Lord! As You have consigned me to perversity (aghwaytanī), I will surely glamorize [evil] for them on the earth, and I will surely pervert them (la-ughwiyannahum) all” (15:39).1 The letter bāʾ in fa-bi-mā indicates either causality or reciprocation. It means: “Because of You casting me into error, I will surely lie in wait…” or “In return to Your casting me into error, I will surely lie in wait…” Some exegetes have suggested that the letter bāʾ here indicates a vow, but this is not correct. Apparently they said this in order to match the current verse with what Satan says elsewhere [with a vow]: He said, “By Your might, I will surely pervert them all” (38:82).

… I will surely lie in wait (la-aqʿudanna, from quʿūd) for them on Your straight path: What is meant here by the verb quʿūd (lit. to sit) is to constantly be present on the path and wait in ambush there in order to lead astray those who travel on this way. The meaning is: “I will surely sit for them [that is, to abduct and despoil them] on Your straight path, which is the level way that leads them to You and to their happiness.” Everyone is necessarily on a journey to God and pursues His straight path [according to their initial makeup and innate nature].

Then I will come at them from their front and from their rear, and from their right and their lef …: This is what Satan will do to the people as he lies in wait on the straight path. He approaches them from all four sides which surround them. The path where Satan lies in ambush for the people is not a physical path, but a spiritual one. Therefore, the sides from which he approaches people are also immaterial, not physical. We can infer these sides from the other verses in the Qur’an about what Satan does: He makes them promises and gives them [false] hopes, yet Satan does not promise them anything but delusion (4:120); That is only Satan frightening his followers (3:175); and do not follow in Satan’s steps (2:168); Satan frightens

1 In verse 15:39 Satan says to God, “Because You cast me into ghayy, I will cast humankind into ghayy.” What Satan does to humankind is that he misleads them and casts them into error. Therefore, since the word appears in the verse twice in apparently the same meaning, what Satan effectively meant was to accuse God for his error. (Trans.)

you of poverty and prompts you to [commit] indecent acts (2:268). Given these and many other similar verses, we can say:

(1) “Their front” refers to future events that lie ahead of them in this life, such as: (a) their hopes and desires which they like to achieve; (b) the pleasures which they seek; (c) the difficulties which they fear and wish to avoid, like becoming poor due to spending in the way of God, or being blamed by others due to entering a certain path—which is in reality good and praiseworthy.1

(2) “Their rear” refers to their children and descendants. People tend to have certain hopes and fears with respect to their children, who will remain and live after them. People effectively feel that they will live indef nitely in this world, because they imagine themselves living through their

children. Therefore, they find the pleasure and pain of their children to be their own pleasure and pain. This motivates them to accumulate wealth and make all preparations for them through any means possible, whether lawful or unlawful. But by so doing, they kill themselves for the sake of their children.

(3) “Their right (yamīn)” means what is auspicious (maymūn) and conducive to their [true and eternal] happiness, which is religion. Satan makes it appealing to them to exaggerate in certain religious acts, and to impose on themselves certain practices that have not been commanded by God. This is what God calls “following the footsteps of Satan.”2 (4) “Their lef ” is the opposite of “their right”; it refers to Satan decorating indecency and wrong in the eyes of people. He tempts them to

disobey God, commit sins, and pursue their desires.

Al-Zamakhsharī says in al-Kashshāf:

You might ask about the difference between the two prepositions used in this verse, where the verse uses min (from) for “front” and “back” but ʿan (from) for “right” and “lef .”

The answer is that both prepositions are used to introduce the place or location of the verb “come” in the verse. There is more than one preposition used to introduce the place where a verb occurs (called mafʿūl fīhi), just as there is more than one preposition used to make a verb transitive and introduce its object (called

1 For example, deciding to dedicate one’s life to pursuing the path of religious knowledge, or to waging jihad in God’s way. (Trans.)

2 See verses 2:168, 2:208, 6:142, 24:21. (Trans.)

mafʿūl bihi). We should take these from how Arabs employ their language; these things are not open to comparison and logical inference. We can only discuss whether a preposition is used properly or not [according to the common usage and convention of Arabs]. For instance, the verb “sit” is used with two prepositions: (1) “he sat ʿalā (over) his right”; and (2) “he sat ʿan (by) his right.” The former is used when someone sits on the right side of someone in a way that he has a dominant position over him and overshadows him. The latter is used when the person sits next to a person with some distance between them, without touching him. However, due to frequent usage, the latter is also used in other meanings [where there is no distance between the two individuals]. This is similar to the word taʿāl, which we discussed before.1 … and You will not find most of them to be grateful: Here Satan states the outcome of what he is planning to do with humankind: I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will come at them… (7:16-17). Elsewhere in the Qur’an, God describes this in a different way. Instead of saying and You will not find most of them to be grateful, Satan says: Do You see this one whom You have honoured above me? If You respite me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely destroy his progeny, [all] except a few

(17:62). As we see, there too Satan excludes “a few” from his temptation and deception, much like what we see in the current verse. In two other places Satan says: I will surely pervert them all,except Your chosen servants among them (15:39-40, 38:82-83).

Matching these verses shows that “the grateful” (al-shākirīn) in the current verse are the same as “the chosen ones” (al-mukhlaṣīn) [in verses 15:40 and 38:83]. We can indeed confirm this if we deeply reflect on what the two terms mean. Mukhlaṣūn are those who are purely dedicated to God and exclusively chosen by Him. This means that their servitude and

1 The entire quotation from al-Zamakhsharī pertains purely to the Arabic of the verse. His point is that even though two different prepositions are used in the verse (min and ʿan), they convey the same meaning. Taʿāl literally means “come up, ascend” in the imperative, and was originally used to call someone when the caller was in a higher position. Notwithstanding its provenance, it was later used to simply mean “come,” which is what it means nowadays and is also what it means in the Qur’an. (Trans.)

worship are only for God, without associating any partners with Him whatsoever. No one other than God has any share of them. All they care about is God; they have forgotten everything and everyone other than their Lord, including themselves. There is nothing in their heart other than God. They lack the required medium for Satan and his temptations. Shākirūn are those in whom the quality of gratefulness is rooted and established.1 W henever they use anything, they express—verbally and practically—that what they have is from their Lord, Who has blessed them with that bounty. This is the meaning of gratefulness. As a result, they are constantly mindful of their Lord in their dealings with anything, including themselves and others. They see every being as a possession of God

in its entirety, without having any independent control over any aspect of its existence. This is their mind-set before, during, and after they deal with anything or anyone. Since they are mindful of their Lord in such a manner, they have no room to be mindful of others. After all: Allah has not put two hearts within any man (33:4).

Given the above explanations, if we analyze the true meaning of the two terms, “the grateful” (al-shākirīn) are the same as “the chosen ones” (al-mukhlaṣīn), who are necessarily exempt from Satan’s deceptions and temptations. He has no way to mislead them because they lie outside his purview. Therefore, the exclusion of these people from Satan’s temptations is based on their real characteristics, not based on some decision by

Satan who could have decided otherwise. It is not a favor and kindness of Satan to some humans.

Satan said to the Almighty God: As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path… and You will

not find most of them to be grateful (7:16-17). He said that he will assault humankind from every possible angle and will cast them into perdition by leading them away from the straight path. However, he did not explain how he operates and what he will do to achieve this. Nevertheless, we can infer two points from what he said:

(1) He will deceive and mislead humankind by means of his own perversity—which he claimed to be an act of God. In other words, he

1 This means that shākir here serves as ṣifah mushabbahah (also called ṣifah mushbihah), which is an adjective that is similar to an active participle. It serves as an adjective, and indicates the establishment, subsistence, and strength of a quality in the subject. (Trans.)

approaches the people with his perverted soul, which means that what he transmits to them is perversity. This is like a fire that is placed next to some water: the fire heats up the water by its own heat. We can clearly see this idea in the following verses: Muster the wrongdoers and their mates and what they used to worship… Some of them will turn to others, questioning each other. They will say, “Indeed you used to accost us peremptorily.” They will answer, “Rather, you [yourselves] had no faith… So we perverted you, for we were perverse [ourselves]” (37:22 and 37:27-29).

(2) What Satan affects in humankind is their mental faculty of conception and confirmation of what should and should not be done. This is the

nature of Satan’s activity and interaction with humans.1 We will elaborate on this in our discussion below on Iblīs and his function.

(7:18) Said He, “Begone hence, blameful (madhʾūman), banished (madḥūran)! Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill hell with you all.”

The adjective madhʾūm (in the accusative case) is derived from the verb dhāmahu yadhāmuhu yadhīmuhu, which is used when someone reproaches and disparages someone. The adjective madḥūr (in the accusative case) is derived from the verb daḥarahu, which is said when someone

repels and rejects someone with humiliation and degradation.

…Whoever of them (la-man) follows you…: The letter lām here indicates vow [for emphasis]. The complement of the vow is: I will surely fill

hell… Satan said this as a threat to take revenge against humankind. While the purpose of their creation was for them to be grateful, Satan claimed that he would not let that materialize. Since Satan’s statement revolved around humankind, God also replied by first outlining what He will do to humankind: Whoever of them follows you. But then He also included Satan in His punishment in what follows next: I will surely fill hell with you (minkum) all, where the plural pronoun “you” refers to Satan and

1 This point is apparently inferred from what is narrated from Satan elsewhere in the Qur’an, where he talks about embellishing the pleasures of this life and prolonged hopes in the sights of humankind (4:119-120, 15:39, 17:64). (Trans.) his followers among humans. This last part of the verse also bears a sign of God’s mercy and grace, because instead of including all of Satan’s followers, He said minkum (of you, from you), where the particle min (of,

with, from) is partitive.1

(7:19) [Then He said to Adam,] “O Adam, dwell with your mate in paradise, and eat thereof whence you wish; but do not approach this tree, lest you should be among the wrongdoers (al-ʿālimīn, from ẓulm).”

Here God specifically addresses Adam, but then adds his wife in His directive.

… and eat thereof whence you wish…: Although this statement is in the form of a command, it indicates permissibility [not obligation] of consuming everything except what is excluded: but do not approach this tree.

What is meant here by ẓulm (wrongdoing, injustice, oppression) is wronging and hurting oneself, not disobeying an authoritative command, because what God said was rather an advisory command.2

1 The meaning would be: “Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill hell with some of you.” However, this interpretation clearly contradicts the word “all” (ajmaʿīn) at the end of the verse. Therefore, the particle min is prefatory (ibtidāʾiyyah) not partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah). The translation above is according to this more apparent and coherent interpretation. (Trans.)

2 An “authoritative command” (al-amr al-mawlawī) is like what a master says to his servant, where the servant is accountable for fulfilling the master’s command, and the master will mete out punishment to the servant if he disobeys. An “advisory command” (al-amr al-irshādī) is like a prescription that a doctor gives a patient. The doctor only informs the patient that if he does not follow the prescription, he will suffer pain or death as a consequence of his disobedience, not that the doctor would come and inflict that suffering as a punishment. The patient is not responsible toward the physician as the servant is toward the master. In both types of command, disobedience results in a painful consequence, but they differ in terms of responsibility and classification. (Trans.)

(7:20) Then Satan tempted (fa-waswasa) them, to expose to them what was hidden (wūriya, from muwārāh) from them of their shameful parts (sawʾātihimā), and he said, “Your Lord has only forbidden you from this tree lest you should become angels, or lest you become immortal.”

Waswasah means “prompting someone to an act with a sofiiquiet voice.” Muwārāh means “concealing something by placing it behind something that covers it.” Sawʾāh is the plural of sawʾah, which means “a body

part that would disgrace and distress (yasūʾu) the person if it were to be revealed and seen.”

… Your Lord has only forbidden you from this tree lest you should become (an takūnā) angels (malakayn)…: The literal meaning here is, “Your Lord has only forbidden you from this tree in order that you become angels or become immortal”; however, the implied meaning is: “in order to avoid that you become angels or become immortal.”1 The common recitation of the verse is with the word malak (angel, in its dual form malakayn), but it also implies mulk (kingdom, sovereignty) based on the verse: He [Satan] said, “O Adam! Shall I show you the tree of immortality, and an imperishable kingdom (mulk)?” (20:120).

Majmaʿ al-bayān has narrated from the late al-Sayyid al-Murtaḍá:

Another possible interpretation for what Satan said—lest you should become angels…—is that he suggested to Adam and Eve that the prohibition on eating from the tree is only applicable to the angels and the immortals, not to them. This is like when we say, “You have not been prohibited this unless you are so-andso” (mā nuhīta ʿan kadhā illā an takūna fulānan), where what we

mean is that “only so-and-so has been prohibited.” This makes Satan’s deception stronger and more cunning.

However, we should reject the above possibility based on the verse from Sūrah Ṭā-Hā [20:120], which we just quoted above.

1 In other words, the word karāhata (to avoid, being unwilling) is implied in the verse. This is already incorporated in the translation above. (Trans.)

(7:21) And he swore to them (qāsamahumā, from muqāsamah), “I am indeed your well-wisher (al-nāṣiḥīn, from nu.).”

Muqāsamah [from the root qasam (vow, swear), in the verbal pattern mufāʿalah] indicates exaggeration in vow and swearing. Nuṣḥ (sincerity, honesty, sympathy) is the opposite of ghishsh (deception, cheating). The meaning is: “Satan swore to them and accentuated that he only wishes them well and gives them good counsel.”

(7:22) Thus he brought about their fall (fa-dallāhumā, from tadliyah) by deception (bi-ghurūr). So when they tasted of the tree, their shameful parts became exposed to them, and they began to stitch (yakhṣifāni, from khaṣf) over themselves with the leaves of paradise. Their Lord called out to them, “Did I not forbid you from that tree, and tell you that Satan is indeed your manifest enemy?”

Tadliyah means “to bring something closer to something else and make it reach the other thing.” It is similar to tadallī, which is “to be loosened and drop down.” Apparently these terms are used metaphorically,

derived from the idea of suspending and sending down a bucket, where one says: dalawtu al-dalw (I unleashed the bucket). Ghurūr means “to express well-wishing while intending to cheat.” Khaṣfiis “to gather and join.” One of its usages is khaṣfial-naʿl (cobbling, shoemaking, stitching a shoe).

… Their Lord called out (nādāhuma, frim nidāʾ) to them, “Did I not forbid you from that (tilkumā) tree, and tell you that Satan is indeed your manifest enemy?”:Nidāʾ means “calling from a distance.” The use of this term shows that at this point Adam and Eve were far from their Lord. Likewise, tilkumā (that) is a demonstrative pronoun that is used for objects at a distance. This shows that they were also distanced from the forbidden tree, unlike the beginning of their entrance into the garden, when God told them: but do not approach this tree (7:19) [where the demonstrative pronoun “this” (hādhihi) indicates an object that is near].

(7:23) They said, “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves! If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.” This prayer by Adam and Eve shows their utmost level of humility and earnest petition before their Lord, such that they did not explicitly request anything. They only expressed their dire need for God’s forgiveness and mercy, and the risk of their eternal failure. They expressed these

points and lefiithe rest to God’s will.

(7:24) He said, “Get down, being enemies of one another! On the earth shall be your abode and sustenance for some time.”

Apparently the verse has a consistent theme, which means that all its plural pronouns refer to Adam, his wife, and Satan.1 God addresses them with two decrees: (1) They shall be enemies of one another—according to their evident difference of nature and makeup. (2) They shall have an abode on the earth until the end of the life of this world (dunyā).

(7:25) He said, “In it you will live, and in it you will die; and from it you will be raised [from the dead].”

This is a third decree that God made, but it is likely that this was specifically addressed to Adam, Eve, and their descendants, because the verse is separated from the last verse by the repetition of the word qāla (He said) [which could have been lefiiout]. God decreed that they should be bound on the earth until the Resurrection. We discussed the story of Adam’s garden elaborately in Sūrah al-Baqarah. Interested readers should refer to there.2

Iblīs and his Function

Unfortunately, the topic of Iblīs (Satan, the Devil) has become vulgarized among us. We do not pay any serious attention to it—other than

mentioning him here and there by cursing him, seeking refuge in God from him, and describing our evil thoughts as being Satanic and a result of his temptations and whispers. However, we do not tend to contemplate what the Qur’an says about the reality of this strange creature which is hidden from our senses. His authority and impact on human life is truly stupendous.

Satan is certainly a wondrous creature, for he has been present in the human world despite its vastness, ever since the onset of its existence. And he will continue to be with humans all the way until the end of this realm, when the world’s spread is rolled up. Then he will continue to be with some humans after their death, until he submits them to hell forever. He is with each and every single one of us while being with others as well. He accompanies us both outwardly and inwardly, penetrating to the most hidden imaginations that we entertain in our mind and the thoughts that are hidden in our inmost secret. He is not veiled from us by anything, nor is he engaged by anything from attending to us.

Muslim scholars have neglected going into any depth on this topic.

They have predominantly pursued the line of discussion presented by the scholars in the early years of Islam, which consists of simple points that spring in the minds of the public when they first hear about Satan in the Qur’an. Every sect has understood his story in its own [superficial] way, has set that as a bulwark to defend its principles, and has drawn on it to quarrel against the other sects through polemical debate. Their discussions are limited to listing various questions and objections that are raised

regarding the story, elaborating the problems, and then answering them from different dimensions.

Some examples of these questions are:

(1) Why did God create Iblīs to begin with, even though He knew who this creature is [and will be]?

(2) Why did God join Iblīs with the angels, even though he was not one of them?

(3) Why did God order Iblīs to prostrate, even though He knew that he would not comply?

(4) Why did God not force him to prostrate, but instead led him astray?

(5) Why did God not kill Iblīs when he did not prostrate?

(6) Why did God give Iblīs respite till the day they will be resurrected [7:14, 15:36, 38:79] or until the day of the known time [15:38, 38:81]? (7) Why did God give Iblīs such an amazing reign over humankind, such that he flows in them like blood? Why did God provide Iblīs with infantry and cavalry [17:64]? Why did God give him access to every aspect of human life?

(8) Why did God not make Iblīs’ workings on humankind sensible to them, so that they may protect themselves against his

temptations?

(9) Why did God not give to humankind the same power over Iblīs as he gave to Iblīs over humankind?

(10) Why did God not conceal the details and secrets of the creation of Adam and his descendants from Iblīs so that he may not wish to mislead them?

(11) How was it possible for Iblīs to talk to God, even though he was neither a prophet nor an angel, but was the most distant and hated creation to God? In response to this, some have said that it was a miracle (muʿjizah) that he spoke with God. Others have said that he spoke indirectly by creating some signs that conveyed what he meant. However, there is no evidence to prove either of these views.

(12) How did Iblīs enter paradise [that is, Adam’s garden]?

(13) How could there be temptation, sin and lying in paradise, even though it is a place of purity and sanctity?

(14) How come Adam accepted what Iblīs said, even though it was contrary to what God had told him?

(15) How could Adam be tempted by kingdom and eternity [in this world; 20:120], even though that is against the belief in the hereafter [which implies that nothing in this world lasts]?

(16) How could Adam sin even though he was an infallible prophet?

(17) How come when God accepted Adam’s repentance, he was not taken back to his original position? Is it not true that “one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin”1?
