And the list continues. In response to such questions, here is a list of what exegetes have said with respect to this story. Here we can clearly trace their unfounded polemical debates, and their negligence in doing justice to this topic:

(1) The entire story is absolutely imaginative, where Adam is a representation of humankind [otherwise, there was no real person

called Adam].

(2) W hat the Qur’an calls “Iblīs” is rather our evil inclinations and temptations [not an external entity].

(3) There is no rational problem with ascribing evil and wickedness to God. Rather, all sins are His acts. He creates evil and ruins His own creation. Good is whatever He commands, and evil is whatever He prohibits.

(4) Adam was not a prophet.

(5) Prophets are not infallible in any point in their life.

(6) Prophets are not infallible before they are chosen as prophets. In this case, the story of the garden occurred before Adam was appointed a prophet.

(7) This story was nothing but a test and trial [by God]. However, the advocates of this claim have not identified the standard [of success] in this huge test, which has led many people into error and fatality.

If we do not have a clear principle to treat this issue at the grass roots, all of the above objections would rise again.

A fundamental problem that the scholars have fallen into with respect to this topic is failing to distinguish between what pertains to ḥaqīqah (existential reality, external world) and what pertains to iʿtibār (social convention, mental construction). They have not discerned the difference between the realm of takwīn (creation, causation, existence) and the realm of tashrīʿ (legislation, injunction). As a result, they have often applied legislative principles to creational matters, while they are only applicable as social contracts. This has ruined their entire discussion.

Clarifying the Problem

To do justice to this topic without any prejudice, we must make note of three principles:

(1) The existence of anything—in and of itself, and regardless of its relation with other things—can only be good. Evil is only relational. Otherwise, what is created and brought into existence is always good. This is a direct consequence of the meaning of “existence.” Suppose that something which is evil in its essence were to be created. Once it is created, it is an “existent” with certain existential properties. In and of itself,

it will be an existent that has come from God, is sustained by Him, and returns to Him. In this sense, it is no different from any other being and has no element of evil in it. Evil comes into play only when we consider the relationship between one being with other beings, where it may contravene a fair order in the world or cause some deprivation for another

being. That is what is meant when we say that evil is necessarily a relative or relational property.

We can further add that whatever we consider to be evil in the world, must have benefits that necessarily exceed its harm. Otherwise, its creation would be against God’s wisdom and the robust order of the universe. The Qur’an says: He has perfected everything that He has created (32:7); Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all nations (7:54); There is not a thing but celebrates His praise, but you do not understand their glorification (17:44).

(2) Even though the world of creation is enormously vast and consists of numerous parts, all these parts are linked to one another, and compose a consistent whole. This means that to create some part is to create the rest, and to fix one part is to fix the whole. What makes this world this world, is that it is composed of disparate constituents. Diversity and disparity are part and parcel of this world. A necessary implication of this,

according to divine wisdom, is that the constituting parts of this world have a variety of harmonious and disharmonious relationships with one another. They stand at different levels of perfection or imperfection, possession or deficiency, achievement or failure. If there were no difference

between them, then they would no longer be many, and their multitude would collapse into a single unit without any distinction or discrepancy. Then this world would no longer exist. God says: and Our command is but a single [word], like the twinkling of an eye (54:50).1 This means that if there were no evil properties such as corruption, weariness, privation, imperfection and weakness, there would be no

1 In other words, an essential property of this world is multiplicity, and multiplicity, by definition, necessitates difference. Verse 54:50 refers to a single

command which marks the end of this realm of multiplicity. (Trans.) instance of good properties such as health, comfort, possession and perfection. Had there been no instance of these things, we could not infer

their meanings either, because we construct mental concepts based external instances. Likewise, if there were no misery, there would be no felicity; if there were no disobedience, there would be no obedience; if there

were nothing to blame, there would be nothing to praise; if there were no punishment, there would be no reward; and if there were no world, there would be no hereafter.

To show this, we can look at the case of obedience as an example.

Obedience means complying with an authoritative command (al-amr al-mawlawī). However, this is only meaningful if there is also the possibility of disobedience. Otherwise, one’s act would be necessary and

inevitable. If one’s acts occur out of necessity, authoritative commands would be meaningless, because it is logically impossible to acquire what has already been acquired (taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil). If there is no authoritative command, there will be no instance of obedience, and without any instance

of obedience, there will be no concept of it, as we explained above. Then, if there is no obedience or disobedience, there will be no place for praise or blame, which are consequent to them. Likewise, there would be no room for reward, punishment, promise, threat, encouragement or warning. This would make void the call and laws of religion in their entirety,

as well as prophethood and messengership. Without these, there would be no society or civilization, without which there would be no humanity, and that would mean the collapse of the entire system of creation. The same analysis can be applied to all other dichotomies in the world. The reader should reflect on this.1

1 Having a non-dualistic view of life (called Advaita) will lead to transcending choice, having no preference, and going beyond good and evil. There is only a single whole, which is the reality, which manifests in different forms of good and bad, pleasant and unpleasant, obedience and disobedience. If we realize that these dichotomies are two sides of the same coin of creation and existence, that one is inseparable from the other because they are parts of the same whole, then we can make a breakthrough to mystical detachment and indifference, which is a foundation for spiritual liberation. This detachment is zuhd (disinterestedness) in its advanced level, where zuhd is not the opposite of materialism, but it is the opposite of duality and distinction. It is to transcend the opposites and behold their underlying oneness without any preference. (Trans.)

Given the above explanation, it should be clear that the existence of Satan—as a force that pulls toward evil and disobedience—is part of the structure of the human world, which pursues human perfection through free will. Humans have a path to follow laboriously until they meet their Lord [84:6]. If we think of the straight path as a road, Satan’s position would mark the sides or shoulders of this road. Evidently, one cannot define the center of a road if it has no borders which surround it from the outside. If there are no sides, it is also meaningless to have a center. The reader should reflect on this in the light of these verses: He [Iblīs] said: “As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path” (7:16); He [God] said, “This is a straight path incumbent upon Me. Indeed as for My servants you do not have any authority over them, except the perverse who follow you” (15:41-42).

If you reflect on the above two points, as well as the verses about the prostration of the angels and Satan to Adam, then you will realize that the story discussed in these verses is about a real relationship that exists between humans, angels and Satan. In order to depict their positions with respect to one another, the Qur’an talks about God’s command [to prostrate to Adam], the compliance [of the angels], the defiance of Satan, and his subsequent expulsion, banishment and conversation with God. All objections with respect to this story are due to not contemplating it fully. For instance, one exegete1 has rightly realized that the verses refer to the nature of humankind, angels and Satan. However, he has wrongly interpreted God’s command and prohibition in this story—that is, God’s command to Satan to prostrate, and His prohibition of Adam from eating from the tree—as takwīnī (existential, creational, causal) orders. This

contradicts his previous observation. It has eluded him that God’s takwīnī orders cannot be violated, while Iblīs disobeyed God’s command, and Adam disobeyed His prohibition.

(3) As we discussed under the verses in Sūrah al-Baqarah [2:30ff], this story refers to a garden in barzakh (the intermediate realm between this life and the Resurrection), which God created for a special purpose. While Adam was to be charged with religious obligation and authoritative commands in his earthly life, God placed him first in that garden

in order reveal some facts about human nature by testing it. That stage

1 Tafsīr al-manār, volume 8, under the current verses, titled “Questions Concerning the Story” (al-ishkālāt fīal-qiṣṣah). (Auth.)

was meant to show the need of humans to experience life on earth. They must be exposed to God’s commands and prohibitions throughout their life on earth. If they comply, they will qualify for the [eternal] Garden. If not, they will not. This is humakind’s way to attain divine proximity and eternal bliss.

The above points should clarify that none of the objections that the exegetes have raised about the story of the garden is applicable. First, the garden was not one of the eternal gardens in the hereafter. In the hereafter, only the friends of God are admitted to paradise, and they will never

leave it after their entry. Second, the garden was not in this world either, in the sense that it was not governed by authoritarian commands and prohibitions. It was not of a nature of this world, where religious obligation is applicable. Rather, it was a place to manifest human nature, and

this brings us to our third observation: the story is not about Adam as an individual, but as a representative of all humans. He was placed in that garden because he was a human, and the angels and Satan were ordered to prostrate themselves before him as a human. We have already explained all these points.

Back to Iblīs

God does not give us much detail about the essence of this evil creature called Iblīs. The Qur’an describes Iblīs as follows: He [Iblīs] was one

of the jinn, so he transgressed against his Lord’s command (18:50), and narrates from him: You created me from fire (7:12). This shows that he is of the

kind of the jinn, and the main element in his creation was fire. The Qur’an does not elaborate the stages of his creation as it discusses the creation of humankind in detail. There are, however, some verses that can reveal some more information about Iblīs. For instance, God narrates from him: I will surely lie in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will come at them from their front and from their rear, and from their right and their lef , and You will not find most of them to be grateful (7:16-17). Here he proclaims that he will get a hold of humankind through their psychological traits and emotions such as fear, hope, ambition, plans, lust and anger. Thus he will influence their thoughts and decisions which are based on these feelings. Another example is: My Lord! As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely glamorize [evil] for them on the earth (15:39). This means that he makes vain, foul and indecent acts appear appealing to humankind by embellishing them with various adornments and attractions, as a means of leading them astray. For instance, one imagines fornication and finds it appealing because of his lust, such that its indecency and evil consequences become faint in his mind, to the point that he confirms his lust

and commits the act. Other similar verses are: He [Satan] makes them promises and gives them [false] hopes, yet Satan does not promise them anything but delusion (4:120); But Satan made their deeds seem decorous to them (16:63).

As the readers can see, all these verses indicate that the sphere of Satan’s activity is human cognition, and his means of operation are feelings and emotions. He entices the passions of the people and appeals to

their sentiments. He infuses false ideas and vain illusions into the human soul, as the Qur’an says: who puts temptations into the breasts of humans, from among the jinn and humans (114:5-6). Meanwhile, we find these ideas and imaginations—which we call “the whispers and temptations of the Devil” (wasāwis, sing. waswasah)—to be our own thoughts, without having any doubts about it. We do not sense anyone imparting them to us from outside. Nor do we acquire them through an intellectual process. Rather, we find them readily available to us, much like statements such as “one is half of two” and “four is even.”

There is no contradiction between saying that these ideas and imaginations are our own, and saying that Satan inspires them to our mind. The

thing is that Satan’s involvement here is not like the involvement of other people who give us some information or command us to do something.

If it were of that sort, then we would no longer have independence of thought, and our acts would no longer be called voluntary, because they ensue from the knowledge, preference and will of Satan, not us. Then there would be no blame or censure on us for our misdeeds. However, Satan himself holds us responsible for our deeds on the Day of Resurrection, as God narrates from him: When the matter is all over, Satan will say, “Indeed Allah made you a promise that was true and I [too] made you a promise, but I failed you. I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot respond to your distress calls, neither can you respond to my distress calls. Indeed I disavow your taking me for [Allah’s] partner aforetime.

There is indeed a painful punishment for the wrongdoers” (14:22). Here he describes humans as actors and wrongdoers who should bear the blame, and exonerates himself of that. Satan denies of himself all authority except as much as calling and making false promises. Likewise, God states that he has no authority over anyone except for those who follow him: Indeed as for My servants you do not have any authority over them, except the perverse who follow you (15:42). Elsewhere He says [about the sinner]: His companion [that is, Satan] will say, “Our Lord! I did not make him a rebel, but he [himself] was in extreme error” (50:27).

Overall, the role of the person and the role of Satan in the cognitive process have a ṭūlī relationship (vertical, longitudinal, causal), meaning that they belong to two planes of existence, where one is a cause or means for the other. Hence, Satan’s involvement in this process is compatible with the involvement of the person, and the resulting act can be rightly attributed to both. Satan’s acts do not have an ʿarḍī relationship (horizontal, latitudinal, parallel) with our acts, meaning that he does not operate

at the same plane as we do. If that were the case, then any act could either be attributed to us or to him, but not to both.1 Satan influences our cognition in all our affairs and dealings in this world, through deception and adornment. He presents falsehood to us in place of truth, such that we deal with things only through their illusory aspect, which is deceptive and bars us from the truth. More precisely, his deception and adornment is that he makes us perceive ourselves and other things in life to be independent entities. This view prevents us from realizing the Truth, and distracts us from real life. As we said, this can be deduced from what the Qur’an narrates from him: As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely lie in wait for them (7:16); My Lord! As You have consigned me to perversity, I will surely glamorize [evil] for them on the earth (15:39). This boils down to being heedless of God (ghafiah), which is

1 A vertical (ṭūlī) relationship can be compared to concentric circles, where a point can be inside both and rightly attributed to both of them. A horizontal (ʿarḍī) relationship can be compared to mutually exclusive circles, where there is no overlap between them. The distinction between vertical and horizontal relationships is key to understanding free will despite the deterministic system of causes and effect. In the case of God, the matter is more profound and subtle, because even the existence and acts of Satan are vertically tied to Him. This is the metaphysical solution. There is yet a mystical explanation, which lies in the idea of tajallī (manifestation, epiphany, divine expression). For more on vertical and horizontal relationships, see my footnote on volume 16, pp. 6-7. (Trans.)

the root of every sin. God says: Certainly We have created for hell many of the jinn and humans: they have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, they have ears with which they do not hear. They are like cattle; rather, they are more astray. It is they who are the heedless (7:179).

So we can say that Satan is the source of this sense of independence and being unmindful of God, which results in all kinds of false beliefs, illusions, polytheism and wrongdoing. Meanwhile, since one feels himself to be independent, he imagines that this very impression has arisen from himself and belongs to him! This shows how pervasive Satan’s machination is, such that it leaves its mark on any subsequent view or practice that

the person may have. This is how one goes under the authority, direction and influence of Satan, without realizing any force being involved beyond oneself. Thus God says: Indeed he sees you—he and his hosts—whence you do not see them. We have indeed made the devils guardians of those who have no faith (7:27).

It should be noted that Satan’s authority over humans with respect to theirs sins and wrongdoing is like the authority of angels over them with respect to their obedience and good deeds, as the Qur’an describes: Indeed those who say, “Our Lord is Allah!” and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, [saying,] “Do not fear, nor be grieved! Receive the good news of the paradise which you have been promised. We are your friends in the life of this world” (41:30-31). The Devil and the angels operate at the same plane, while God, above all, is the ultimate authority without any rival. And Allah besieges them from all around (85:20); You do not have besides Him any guardian or intercessor (32:4).

This is the bit and rein of Satan which God describes elsewhere: Said he [Satan], “Do You see this one whom You have honored above me? If You respite me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely rein his progeny, [all] except a few.” Said He, “Begone! Whoever of them follows you, indeed the hell shall be your requital, an ample reward. Entice whomever of them you can with your voice; and rally against them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them!” But Satan promises them nothing but delusion (17:62:64). The meaning is: “I shall reign over them by putting a rein and bit on them, just as a rider controls the horse by pulling the bridle. Hence they will obey me in whatever I command them, and will turn toward wherever I direct them, without any resistance or disobedience whatsoever.”

We can also deduce from the verses of the Qur’an that Satan has certain hosts and armies which assist him, obey his commands, and help him

achieve what he wants. As we quoted above, the Qur’an says: Indeed he sees you—he and his hosts—whence you do not see them (7:27). Regardless of how many these hosts are and how diverse their activities may be, they work under the umbrella of Iblīs. Their work is his work, and their temptations are his, as he ascribes this to himself in several verses such as: I

will surely pervert them all (15:39). This is much like the case of the angels, where there are some archangels who have many assistants which operate under their direction. The acts of the subordinates are imputable to their superiors. For instance, God says concerning the Angel of Death and his subordinates: Say, “You will be taken away by the angel of death, who has been charged with you. Then you will be brought back to your Lord” (32:11); When death approaches anyone of you, Our messengers take him away and they do not neglect [their duty] (6:61).

There are a few points about the hosts of Satan which we can infer from the Qur’an:

(1) Who puts temptations into the breasts of humans, from among the jinn and humans (114:5-6). This shows that the hosts of Satan include both humans and jinn.

(2) Will you then take him and his offspring for guardians in My stead, though they are your enemies? (18:50). This verse shows that part of Satan’s hosts are his descendants, but the Qur’an does not give us any more information about the process of their procreation.

(3) And rally against them your cavalry and your infantry (17:64).

According to this verse, his soldiers differ in terms of strength and speed of operation. That is the difference between cavalry and infantry, where one is more swifiiand effective in operations.

(4) And say, “My Lord! I seek Your protection from the promptings of devils; and I seek Your protection, my Lord, from their presence near me”

(23:97-98). This suggests that some devils work in groups, while others work individually. Perhaps we can also deduce the same point from these verses: Should I inform you on whom the devils descend? They descend on every sinful liar. They eavesdrop, and most of them are liars (26:221-223). Summary

Iblīs is a real being who was created by God, is possessed of intelligence and will, and prompts the people to disobey God. Until before

the creation of Adam, Satan was at the same level as the angels, without any distinction between them. After that, there was a split between Satan and the angels, where Satan chose the side of evil and mischief. Certain acts of humankind—such as their deviation from the straight path, their inclination to error and wretchedness, and their pursuit of falsehood and disobedience—can be ascribed to Satan in one way or another. He can be compared to the angels, who are also creatures with intelligence and will. Angels too can be credited, in one way or another, with certain acts of humankind, including their achievement of ultimate happiness, perfection, and the abode of divine proximity.

Satan has a diverse set of hosts among the jinn, the humankind, and his progeny. They follow his command and influence all worldly affairs and dealings of humankind. Their job is to present falsehood in the form of truth, and decorate what is foul and evil as fair and good. Their fields of operation include both the physical and psychological aspects of human life. They affect every aspect of the people’s worldly life, such as wealth, children and so on. They work in many diverse ways, collectively and individually, quickly and slowly, directly and indirectly. We can arguably add that their influence is not limited to evil and disobedience, but may also include good deeds and obedience.

Meanwhile, one does not feel the involvement and influence of the devils in anything that they do. Instead, one only sees oneself and one’s own acts. This shows that the devils are not at the same level of existence as us, and they do not operate at the same plane as we do. All we know is what God has informed us: that Iblīs is one of the jinn, was created from fire, and had a change of course from his initial position.

The Objections of Satan against the Angels: A Qur’anic and Rational Discussion

Which is yours, I agree;

But why spill my blood?

This is my plea!

Then Abū Firās improvised:

He said, “If I’m the owner

Then it’s all up to me!”

Detailed Response to Satan’s Objections

Our explanations above would answer all of these six objections, without needing the entire creation to gather from the beginning to the end—

as al-Imām [al-Rāzī] has claimed—and still being unable to solve them. For further clarification, we shall discuss the six questions one by one: (1) The first objection is about the wisdom behind God’s creation. This refers to the aspect of good and benefit in an act which makes an agent

1 This refers to the historical debate between Ashʿarite and Muʿtazilite theologians concerning the root of moral values and the divine command theory in ethics. (Trans.)

2 Sayfial-Dawlah (d. 967 CE) was the founder of the Emirate of Aleppo. Abū Firās al-Ḥārith b. Saʿīd al-Ḥamdānī (d. 968 CE) was a renowned Arab poet and governor. (Trans.)

perform the act. In the case of God, one can ask about the wisdom behind the creation of all beings in general, or the wisdom behind the creation of humankind in particular.

If the question is about God’s act of creation in general, then it has been proven in its place that God is a perfect agent Who is absolutely needless of anything beyond Himself. He does not depend on anything to complete His agency (fāʿiliyyah) or divinity (ulūhiyyah). He is the origin of everything other than Him and the source of all good and mercy by the virtue of His essence. His very existence necessitates the creation, because one of His essential qualities is that He is the Origin, and it is senseless to demand a reason for a necessary property.1 We can compare this to one who is inherently generous, meaning that generosity has become a malakah (second nature, natural disposition, permanent quality) to him. Such nature necessitates—by the virtue of itself, not by anything external to it—to manifest certain signs, effects and blessings. If it manifests

because of any consideration other than the quality itself, then that would not be a malakah. It is a necessary consequence of this essence to have certain expressions, where everyone would benefit from it according to their receptive capability and capacity. If the containers differ in terms of their capacity to receive blessings, then that difference goes back to them, not to the essential property of the agent, which is only a source of good. It is often said that there must be some wisdom—meaning a purpose or beneficial aspect—in the act of an agent, where the agent does the act for that purpose. In the case of imperfect agents, this would be a benefit that accrues to the agent who lacks it before doing the act, and grows to perfection by achieving that objective. However, in the case of an Agent Who possesses all good and perfection, His purpose in His acts would be His very essence. He is not motivated to act in order to achieve anything beyond Himself, just as we saw in the case of generosity when it becomes an established property in the person. It is true that the acts of such an Agent have numerous benefits, and that God’s blessings never end, but these benefits and blessings are not primary objective that God aims for in His acts [as imperfect agents aim for objectives in their acts]. They are

1 This would be like asking, “Why does x = x?” The answer is: “Otherwise, it would be something else.” It is logically incoherent to demand a cause or reason for an essential property. For the same reason, one cannot demand a reason for what necessarily issues from an essential property. (Trans.) rather secondary objectives and by-products of His agency. This is what we can say about God’s creation overall.1 The question, however, seems to be about the wisdom behind creating humankind, because it points to God’s knowledge that disbelievers

would end up in hell. As we said above, the point in God’s creation cannot be interpreted as something that He gains and benefits from. God

is rich and needless of all things by the virtue of His essence. He is not perfected by achieving anything. What is meant by wisdom in the case of God is the perfection of His act to full fruition. His wisdom in the creation of humankind is to take the abject earthly material and make a special composition of it which will be able to journey toward a degree of perfection that is above the perfection of all other beings in existence. He has created a being of dust which can reach a degree of proximity to his Lord that cannot be achieved by anything else. This is the ultimate purpose of the human species.

Meanwhile, we should bear in mind that this creature is made of earthly material, which [inherently and necessarily] consists of opposites. It grows in a realm of multiplicity and conflict, and is surrounded by favorable and unfavorable phenomena. This entails that not all members of

such a species would be spared of the opposing forces in this life. Hence, only a subset of them will come to fruition and succeed in making it to their desired happy end.

This is nothing exclusive to humankind. Rather, all material beings in this world are like this, including all animals, plants, and inorganic objects. There are millions of various species in this world, and all of them have a certain perfection which they pursue as a species. However, not every member of the species reaches that goal. They achieve their perfection collectively as a species, but not individually. There are many members which perish along the way, due to unfavorable causes and events which stop their growth. They fail to reach the end that is intended for them. We cannot even assume a being in the world of nature which is secure from these opposing factors. All species in the world of nature are surrounded by such factors, and these factors will inevitably have their impact on the

1 In these discussions, benefit (maṣlaḥah), purpose (gharaḍ), objective (ghāyah) and wisdom (ḥikmah) are interdependent and concurrent. An act done out of wisdom is never devoid of some purpose and objective, which is some maṣlaḥah (benefit, betterment, advantage, interest) at some level. (Trans.) species. Suppose a plant that is unaffected by forces that are against its natural composition—such as heat, cold, light, darkness, moisture, dryness, poison and harmful minerals. That would contradict the assumption

that it is a plant with a special natural composition, and also the universal law of causality. Such expectation of a species is against the order of the entire universe [which has the universal law of causality at its core]. If the acts and efforts of some members of a species go to waste, that is not necessarily vain and contrary to wisdom, as long as the entire setup leads other members to their intended goal and perfection, meaning the ultimate end of that species. This is the most that can come out of material creation. Moreover, it is worthwhile to spend large amounts of matter— which is at the base of all planes of existence and the least worthy of them all—in order to acquire a few sublime jewels that top all existential perfections. That would be a real gain rather than a loss or waste of resources.

The objective in the creation of humankind is the perfect human being who reaches the pinnacle of felicity in this world and the next. However, humans are a material species, in that they are composed of matter and exist in the world of nature. This composition means that they are subject to the laws of the material world which govern all beings in the realm of nature. They are born and grow in a realm with various forces at work and different factors that affect each other. A necessary consequence of such a mode of existence is that some members of this species (the homo sapiens) would fail to reach the desired human perfection. Hence, the achievement of maximum human perfection is the primary and essential purpose of creation of humankind, while the failure of some members is intended secondarily as an unavoidable consequence of the first objective. God’s purpose in the creation of humankind is for them to achieve their ultimate perfection. He knows that many of them will be disbelievers and thus end up in hell, but this does not harm His primary objective

in the creation of the entire species. Moreover, what makes someone a disbeliever—and thus subject to punishment in the hereafter—is not the fact that they are created by God, but there are numerous factors which determine this end for a person, the last of which is the person’s choice [to disbelieve and do evil voluntarily]. Because of this element of choice, they are responsible for their disbelief. Their disbelief is a result of several constituent causes, where only some of these constituent causes can be ascribed to their Creator. Finally, one may say that God has indeed willed their disbelief, but God has willed so only through their choice and volition. His will does not render them compelled to act in a certain way—like

a rock that falls toward the earth involuntarily.

(2) Questioning religious obligations on the basis that “no benefit or loss reaches God” is a fallacy because it assumes that the same laws which govern imperfect agents are applicable to a Perfect Agent Who is completely rich and needless in His essence. It is a rule of reason that for any act to be wise and sensible, it must have some benefit for the actor, but this rule is only applicable to imperfect agents which seek to perfect themselves and gain some benefit through their act. It is not applicable to God, Who is assumed to be an essentially needless agent. There is no rational argument for either of the following claims: (i) All agents must derive some benefit from their act, including agents that are needless by the virtue of their essence. (ii) If an agent is needless by the virtue of its essence, then it is impossible for it to perform any act.

Religious obligations pertain to the domain of iʿtibār (convention, social contract, mental construction), which is distinct from the domain of ḥaqīqah (existential reality, external world). Nevertheless, it is through social and religious conventions and laws that the individuals move from one mode of existence to a more complete mode of existence. Hence, religious obligations are a link between two real external entities.1 To further clarify this, we know both experimentally and rationally that all species in the realm of nature are subject to “motion” in its metaphysical sense, meaning that they follow a path that extends from a state

of potentiality to a state of actualization. This connected line of growth is

1 Ḥaqīqī (real) is an adjective for an entity or property that exists in the absence

of a thinking mind. It is something objective that does not depend on a subject to conceive or construct it. Iʿtibārī (conventional, socially constructed,

mentally posited) is an adjective of a concept or proposition that is a result of a mental operation. It exists in the mind of an intelligent subject. The relation between the two can be compared with the relation between objective and subjective. “Good,” “bad,” “saint,” “sinner,” “obedience” and “disobedience” are all labels that our mind applies to external events. What is out there is only that which is. It is an objective occurrence that is neutral with respect to our legal and moral classifications. That is the real existence of any event, and that

is what is attributable to God, Who is absolute existence. Not mixing between the external existence of things and our mental commentaries on them is the key to realizing oneness (tawḥīd). (Trans.)

what marks the continuation and subsistence (baqāʾ) of that being which is ever changing. The different links in this chain of growth have a real and organic connection with one another, such that one leads to the next. The being pursues these links as stages of its growth, and aims toward the final destination from the very onset of its existence.

For example, a grain of wheat is headed toward a full wheat plant from the very beginning when it splits and sprouts. Similarly, the zygote of an animal is on the path to become a mature animal with everything that makes that species complete. The human being is no exception to this universal law. Every individual, from the very beginning of their conception, are directed toward the stage of maximum human perfection and

eternal happiness. Sometimes the beings reach their intended objective, and sometimes their growth is interrupted by certain obstacles.

Now, human beings have a kind of existence that requires them to live socially, and social life is only possible under certain laws and norms that are accepted among the members of the society. This is called social contract. It is a set of conventional views, values and laws, whether rooted in religion or not. Acting in accordance to these principles will develop a set of beliefs and traits in the individuals, which result in their happy life in this world. Likewise, their happiness in the hereafter is a consequence of their adherence to these conventional matters, which results in either reward or punishment.

Hence, the wisdom in religious obligation is that it bears with itself a gradual transformation for humans toward their ultimate perfection, according to their individual traits and personalities. By acting upon these injunctions, they advance step-by-step toward an end that is better and more lasting for them. In case they neglect these instructions, they will fail to achieve that end. In this sense, humankind is just like any other species: they have a path which leads them to their perfection as long as the

means and requirements are there; but if the conditions of their growth are not met, they will not reach their intended goal. If one asks, “what is the point of religious obligation?” it is like asking “what is the point of nourishment for plants?” or “why should animals mate even though it has no benefit [for God]?”

Another part of Satan’s objection was: “God could give any benefit to His creatures directly and without the intermediation of religious obligations.” This is also a fallacy. Based on what we said above, we are talking

about a species whose creation is such that it must follow a gradual path toward perfection. Religious obligations are directed at humans (and other similar beings that are subject to religious legislation)1 because that is their path from potentiality to actualization. They need these injunctions for their existential transformation toward their full development.

Satan’s objection can be interpreted in two ways:

(i) “Why the path of religious obligation and not another path?” We can answer this question in two ways: (a) A destructive answer (al-jawāb al-naqḍī), which would be: “Why not?” That is, there must be some path and intermediation for beings that grow gradually, and any perceivable path would be identical to any other path inasmuch as they are all intermediary stages. If another path had been set for humankind, then one

could equally ask, “Why this path and not another?” (b) A constructive answer (al-jawāb al-ḥallī), saying that the laws and factors which govern humankind are such that they require a set of religious obligations for this species to reach its perfection. They need to purify their souls and purge their inside by persistent adherence to these obligations. Their creation is such that they need these injunctions in order to grow.

(ii) “W hy any intermediation at all? W hy not create them from the beginning in an actualized state, at full perfection and eternal bliss? W hy should there be some movement and gradual growth?” The answer is: That would negate existential transformation, materiality and potentiality, all of which are necessary properties of a contingent creation [in the world of nature]. A being like that would be a being that is created from day one in a state of immateriality, perfection and happiness. That is not the case of humans, which are created from the earth as imperfect beings, which should then actualize their potentialities gradually. In other words, the proposed scenario is self-contradictory.2 (3) Satan said: “Granted that He obligated me to know Him and obey Him, why did He oblige me to prostrate myself to Adam?” The answer to this question is obvious: God’s order served to complete and actualize Satan. If he chose to prostrate himself to Adam, then his quality of servitude and obedience to God would be completed. And if he refused to do

1 Such as the jinn. (Trans.)

2 It is self-contradictory because it is proposed about human beings, but it entails that they should be other beings. Humankind is a material creation, and such creation cannot be divested of gradual transformation. (Trans.) so, then that would manifest his pride and defiance. Either way, this order entails a perfection of a quality in Satan by God, either in the direction of fortune or misfortune. Satan chose the latter.

Moreover, commanding Satan and the angels to prostrate to Adam laid out the straight path which Adam and his descendants should follow. This path requires some helpers who call them to good, which are the angels; and some enemies who call them to deviation and error, which are Satan and his hosts. We already discussed this quality [of the straight path] and these two roles [of angels and devils].1 (4) Satan said: “Why did God curse me and decreed my punishment when I disobeyed His command, even though that does not benefit Him?” The answer is that God’s curse and punishment are not an arbitrary assignment, but they signify a reality. They are an inevitable consequence of

having a sense of arrogance and defiance against God, which is the root of every disobedience. As we said above, God does not act in pursuit of some gain or interest, so it is irrelevant to question His deeds on this account. His objection is like saying: “Why should one who drinks poison die by it? Why doesn’t God make that a source of healing for the person, given that He does not benefit from the person’s death, while the person suffers a great loss? Why doesn’t He make poison quench his thirst, nourish his body, and please his senses?” All these expectations are due to ignorance about the system of cause and effect, which God has placed in the world. Every phenomenon in this world is connected to its specific causes and means, such that it necessarily occurs as a result of those causes, without any change or failure. This is a universal law.

When a soul defiles itself by committing a sin, that act of disobedience necessitates punishment for that soul. This necessary consequence can be avoided only if the soul is purified through repentance, intercession, or a good deed that necessitates an overriding forgiveness. If the punishment is revoked without any of these required means, that would be a violation of the universal law of causality. If this law is violated, then there will be no basis for anything.

(5) Satan said: “When He cursed me, why did He still give me authority over Adam’s children and enable me to deceive and misguide them?”

The answer to this objection should be clear based on what we said above. Obedience, acting upon the truth, and following guidance, only make

The full actualization of a call to truth hinges on the existence of some call to falsehood. If there is to be a straight path, there must be other ways that deviate from the desired destination.

Therefore, as long as there is human life and the species continues to exist through its consecutive generations, there must necessarily be a caller to falsehood who leads the people toward the punishment of hell. This means that Satan serves humankind as a species overall. Besides, the only authority that God has given him is that of calling and tempting the people, as the Qur’an states expressly1 and also narrates from him—when he addresses the people on the Day of Resurrection.2 6) Satan said, “When I requested Him to respite me for such a long time, why did He grant my request?” Our answer to the last objection should clarify this question. He also said, “Clearly a world without evil would have been better.” Again, as we explained above, having a world without evil and corruption means having an immaterial world. This is against the assumption that we are talking about material existence in the world of nature. It is meaningless to have a material world where there is actuality without potentiality, good without evil, gain without loss, stability without change, obedience without disobedience, or reward without

punishment.

God cannot be Questioned about His Actions It was narrated above [in al-Ālūsī’s quote from the commentator of the Gospels] that God responded to Satan’s objections by saying: “O Iblīs! You do not know Me! Had you known Me, you would have realized that no objection can be raised to any of My acts. For indeed I am Allah, there is no god but Me, and I am never held accountable for what I do.” This is a paraphrase of what God says in the Qur’an: He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they are questioned (21:23). Apparently what is narrated from God here is a brief and general response to Satan’s objections,

not a detailed explanation of them one-by-one. It means that all these

points mean calling God into question and objecting to His actions, but He is not liable to any question or objection, because He is God, besides Whom there is no god.

Apparently the second part of God’s answer—that “I am never held accountable”—is stated as a consequence of the first part: “Indeed I am Allah, there is no god but Me.” This amounts to a demonstrative argument which we can elaborate as follows: He is “God,” meaning the Origin and

End of everything. Therefore, one cannot ask for any other agent (fāʿil) or objective (ghāyah) to justify God’s actions. He is the ultimate agent above all agents, and the final end beyond all ends. We cannot assume there to be any other agent behind God’s actions, because that agent would need some power in order to act, while all power belongs to God1. Similarly, We cannot assume there to be any objective in God’s actions besides Himself, because any objective is sought due to some good in it, while all good is in the hands of God2.

That is why He cannot be questioned concerning what He does, because questioning an action means asking either “where did this come from” or “for what purpose was this done?” Neither of these are applicable to God because He is the cause of all causes, and the objective of

all objectives. As with other agents, their power to act comes from God, and any good or interest that they gain is bestowed upon them by God, in the sense that He has set up the system of causes and means which bring one’s objective to fruition. Hence, agents other than God can be questioned why they perform a certain act. The most common questions concerning one’s actions pertain to the purpose of the act, meaning its aspect of good and benefit. This is especially the case with respect to voluntary acts in a social context, where the act can be described as good, bad, praiseworthy and blameworthy, according to how it serves social welfare.

What we said above is a sound explanation [of why God cannot be questioned about His acts], supported by both rational proof and scriptural evidence. The theologians, however, have differed widely on this topic

due to their opposing views about whether or not the acts of God can be justified by a purpose. The Ashʿarite view is that it is possible for God to act arbitrarily, and that one can ascribe evil, sin and misfortune to Him.

2 See verse 3:26. (Trans.)

They hold that God can do whatever He wants, whether His act comprises of some purpose and benefit or not. Human reason cannot judge Him as it judges other agents, where reason dictates that the agent’s action must include some purpose—meaning a benefit that results from that act.

The Muʿtazilite view is that it is impossible for God to do something without a purpose, because that means that God’s acts can be vain and haphazard, which is certainly not true. They hold that God is not questioned concerning what He does because He is All-Wise, meaning that

He bestows upon everyone and everything according to its capacity and worth. Questioning one about their acts pertains to agents whose acts may sometimes be evil, futile or random. However, since God is a wise agent, He is not questioned concerning what He does, while other agents are. This is a lengthy debate that has continued between the scholars from the two parties and other schools for centuries. An elaborate treatment of the topic is beyond the scope of this book. However, I should bring up an important point that would help to clarify the fact of the matter in this regard.

Two Forms of Human Knowledge

We can classify our knowledge into two kinds of propositions:

(1) There are certain propositions which do not pertain to our actions. These are descriptive statements about external truths, regardless of whether we, as individuals and societies, live and act in this world or not. Some examples are: “four is even,” “one is half of two,” “the world exists” and “there is a sun and a moon.” These are either self-evident propositions, or analytic propositions which can be traced back to axioms and

proven thereby.

(2) There are other propositions which pertain to our actions and interactions in this world. These are normative statements which are constructed through social contracts and are applicable to the human world.

We rely on these principles to organize our life in the society, make plans about what we should do, and justify our voluntary acts. These propositions do not reflect the external world as a primary function, unlike the

first type of propositions. It is true that we impose and implement them in the external world, but they are conventional by nature, not real. Some examples are conventional rules and guidelines that we agree upon in our social interactions, governed by titles like “manager,” “head,” “king,” “owner,” and so on. When we say that “Zayd is the head,” we refer to a position that has been assigned a him based on social contract. It is a conventional quality (called iʿtibārī) which exists only in our mind, as opposed to a real attribute (called ḥaqīqī) which has a real referent and instance in the external world. What we have out there is only Zayd as a human. His managerial position is not like real qualities such as his height and color. “Zayd is the head” is not like “Zayd is tall” or “Zayd is black.” We have mentally derived, constructed and conceptualized the title “head” for Zayd from our social institutions. We humans gather to function together because of some common need in life, and then agree to entrust the management of our affairs to Zayd. He is assigned to place everything where it belongs, and direct things according to his discretion. Seeing this setup, we conclude that the relation of Zayd to our group is that of “head” to the body. We assign this title to him in order to maintain the collective functioning of the group and benefit from it.

The title “head” only exists in our mind, not in the external world. However, we treat it as a real quality for the welfare and interest of the society. The same thing applies to all other conventional qualities and titles that we have set up to govern our social life. All of these are constructed and assigned by humans based on social contract, for the functioning of our life in this world. They do not have any corresponding reality or existence beyond the mind.

These are the two types of knowledge. The difference between them is that the first type is derived from the external world and has a real connection with it. Thus it can be called either true or false, based on whether

or not it matches the external reality. “Truth” means that what we have in our mind is exactly the same as what there is in the outside, and vice versa. The second type exists only mentally, without any counterpart in the real world. However, we treat it as a real quality which corresponds to the outside world for the purpose of social welfare and interest (maṣlaḥah). It is hypothetically assumed to have some reality in the external world, even though it really does not.

Saying that “Zayd is the head” based on a social consideration is like saying, “Zayd is a lion” as a figurative expression or a poetic image. Calling him a “head” among people is like a poet calling him a “lion.” The same can be said about anything that is conventionally constructed, including both concepts and propositions. These conventional meanings are a result of a mental making, as opposed to being derived from the outside world and corresponding to an external reality. Nevertheless, they are based on an external reality in another sense: these titles and notion show a certain need and deficiency in humankind which has led them to construct these concepts and laws. It was due to some real material or spiritual goal that humans had to assume these meanings, in order to give direction to their activities, so that they may reach those goals and find happiness thereby. Here is where we can see why social contracts differ from one society to another: it is because they ensue from a need for different goals. For example, there may be many actions and traits that are approved by communities near the North Pole, but not by communities near the equator.

Similarly, there are differences between eastern and western societies, and between urban and rural communities. Moreover, it could be that in a single society, the majority of the people approve of something, while a minority do not. The same can be said about how social roles are viewed and defined in different societies, with respect to rich versus the poor, master versus servant, employer versus the employee, old versus young, male versus female. Meanwhile, there are some conventional laws and matters that are unanimously agreed upon by all societies, such as the necessity of having a social setup to begin with, the goodness of justice, and the evilness of injustice.

Overall, our second type of knowledge also depends on the external world, although it is not a reflection of outside reality, unlike the first type. This means that all our knowledge is based on God’s action, because external reality—which is a source and point of reference for all our propositions—is a creation of God’s. Therefore, when we say, “one is half of two

by necessity,” it means that “God has set this as a fixed relationship between one and two.” Similarly, when we say that “Zayd must be respected as the head” it means that “God has created humans in a way that leads them to assume such conventions and act upon them.” In the same light we can trace all statements to God’s making.

This means that any assertion made by human reason—including theoretical reason and practical reason—is derived from the plane of divine actions and depends on that. In terms of theoretical reason, there is no difference in this regard between propositions that state a fact as a necessity and those that state a fact as a possibility. Likewise, in terms of practical reason, it does not make a difference whether the proposition classifies something as good or evil. The rulings of practical reason are based on beneficial and harmful consequences, which are again part of God’s making.

Our theoretical reason decides what is necessary, possible or impossible; and our practical reason discerns what is good or bad. However, all

of these qualities are derived from the very act of God Himself. So how could our reason take precedence over Him? How could we hold God subject to the rulings of our reason? Any judgment by our reason would confine and qualify God’s absolute essence. This is a most egregious injustice which some theologians [that is, the Muʿtazilites] have committed.

If we let theoretical reason make statements about God, it means that God can be defined. This is impossible in the case of God, because being defined means being subject to external limits that determine the boundaries of something. It is logically impossible for anything to delimit itself;

thus having defining limits means being subject to an external force, to something beyond the thing itself. Likewise, we cannot let practical reason make statements about God, because that implies that there is some

deficiency in God which must be filled with the conventional laws and customs that practical reason assumes. This is based on the function of the two types of human knowledge that we explained above. The reader is encouraged to pause and reflect here.

Nevertheless, it is also a most egregious injustice if we claim that human reason has no way to understand the acts of God, whether His creation [of the universe] or His legislation [of religious laws]. In other words, we cannot dismiss the rulings of our theoretical reason and practical reason [which are inferred from God’s creation and legislation, respectively]. We cannot make any exceptions to rational laws. We shall clarify

this in two stages, according to our two types of knowledge:

(1) In terms of facts, our theoretical reason deduces certain universal laws from God’s action [which is the world of existence]. That is how it proves God’s existence to begin with. Now, having derived this conclusion, we cannot then turn our back to this faculty and reject its other necessary conclusions on the account that our intellect is too inferior to encompass the essence of God or comprehend His attributes. Putting a hold on theoretical reason, some theologians [that is, the Ashʿarites] have argued that

God’s acts are not a necessary consequence of His essence, but are only backed by His will. Some corollaries of this are: (i) God may do or not do any given act. The doing or not doing of any given act has an absolutely equal relation to His essence. (ii) He has no purpose or objective in His acts. (iii) Both good and evil can be ascribed to Him.

The problem is that if we reject our intellect’s capability of discerning and classifying God’s actions [as good and bad, or possible and impossible], then we have rejected its capability of discerning God’s existence

in the first place. Furthermore, this implies a contradiction that is even more problematic, because it means that our rational inferences do not match the source from which they are inferred. It means that we deduce a conclusion from certain premises, then we claim that our conclusions are not applicable to those very premises. This is nothing but sophistry, which leaves no place for any kind of knowledge, and which is also counter-intuitive (it is against our fiṭrah). If any of God’s actions or attributes

could violate our rational principles, it would mean a mismatch between reason and the external world—which is an act of God, while our rational principles are deduced from the external world. If we concede that even one of these certain conclusions which are deduced by our reason could be doubted and rejected, then we must accept that all of our rational inferences could be wrong. This cancels human knowledge altogether, and that

is the meaning of sophistry.

(2) In terms of actions, our practical and normative statements are certain laws and conventions that we mentally construct and assume in order to reach some goal and betterment in life. Any act that is conducive to that felicitous end is classified as good, and our practical reason commands to it. Any act that is an obstacle to that goal is classified as evil and

wrong, and our practical reason prohibits it. In other words, what makes an act good or evil is its contribution or lack of contribution to a certain objective in life. In the first place, we come up with such classifications of good and bad because of some consideration of a certain interest or welfare. We construct our conventional statements—in the form of social laws and contracts—to serve that end in our mind. Hence, in the realm of normative knowledge, it is rather senseless to talk about any law or conventional statement that is neutral toward good and evil, or that is not backed by any objective.

When we talk about God’s legislation, we are talking about the same type and nature of statements that we have in our societies. For example, when we talk about God’s prescriptions, proscriptions, commands,

prohibitions, promises and warnings, they are of the same nature as human prescriptions, proscriptions, commands, prohibitions, promises and warnings. This is obvious. These are conventional meanings that our minds conceive and claim. Meanwhile, mental claims are prone to error, while God is free from that. Therefore, when He makes a legislation— which is a conventional matter with only mental existence—its aspect of uncertainty is on the side of humans only. This is much like God’s statements of wish (tamannī) and hope (tarajjī): they do not indicate any uncertainty on God’s part, but they show ignorance on the part of the audience. Otherwise, His legislations are like our legislations, in the sense that they pertain to humans—as social animals—that have to move from deficiency to perfection and achieve human happiness through the intermediation of their actions. This proves that God’s actions in the realm of legislation are never devoid of some purpose or objective. Good and evil are also applicable to His commands and prohibitions, according to whether they lead to a benefit or a loss.

This should clarify the problem with two statements [made by the Ashʿarites]: (1) “God’s legislations cannot be justified by any objective.” This is like saying: “God has made a path that does not lead to any destination.” The problem is that a “path” by definition is what leads to some

destination, and an “intermediary” is what connects two things at its two ends. (2) “Good is whatever God commands, and evil is whatever God prohibits. Hence, if God commands something that is evil by the necessary rule of reason—such as injustice—then that would be good; and if

He prohibits something that is good by the necessary rule of reason—such as justice—then that would be evil.” This statement is like saying: “If God leads humankind toward their loss and perdition, then that would be their prosperity and happiness; and if He stops them from their true and eternal bliss, then that would transform bliss into wretchedness.”

The Validity of Human Reason

With respect to theoretical reason, which is concerned with declarative statements, the truth is that there is some place for what human reason discerns and states about God. We ascribe to God certain qualities of perfection which we find in ourselves, such as knowledge, power and life. We also ascribe to Him the creation and direction of all beings, and affirm other qualities for Him such as mercy, forgiveness, provision, blessing and guidance. Human reason establishes all of these for God based on demonstration. However, our qualities of perfection are limited, while God

is far exalted above all limits. Any concepts is also limited, because every concept is different from other concepts, which implies a certain demarcation. This contravenes the absoluteness of God’s essence. Hence, human

reason complements its assertions by negating limitation from God. It admits that God is greater than being described by any description, and is far higher than being enclosed by any condition or limit. Therefore, our reason does justice to Him and brings us close to His knowledge through coupling tashbīh (anthropomorphism, comparison, resemblance) with tanzīh (transcendence, incomparability, abstraction). We quoted a few profound sermons from Imam ʿAlī which clarify and prove this point rationally in the clearest way, under our discussion of the verse, They are certainly faithless who say, “Allah is the third [person] of a trinity” (5:73). Readers are encouraged to consult that discussion.1 With respect to practical reason, which is concerned with imperative statements, there is some place for what human reason states about

the legislative acts of God. However, it should be clarified that what God legislates and enacts conventionally are not because of some need on His part. Rather, they are His means of bestowing some benefit and blessing upon humankind, in order to fulfill their needs, for indeed Allah is dispenser of a great grace [2:105, 3:74, 8:29, 57:21, 57:29, 62:4]. Therefore, on

the one hand, there is some purpose and objective behind God’s legislations; while on the other hand this objective pertains to humankind, not

to God. There is always some benefit that justifies God’s command, but the beneficiary is humankind, not God. We explained this point above. This means that we are entitled to inquire about the rational justification and purpose behind God’s legislations, and search for their

underlying good, evil, benefit or loss. However, this does not mean that human reason can impose anything on God as it imposes on humans. We cannot command or prohibit something upon God as either obligatory or forbidden, because He is absolutely needless of achieving any perfection. That is why He is not subject to any command, unlike us. We stand

before Him like servants and subjects before a mighty and powerful king. All of our affairs are in His hands, including our life, death, sustenance, direction, actions, accounts, rewards and punishments. It is in this light

(1) Concerning statements made by theoretical reason [which are factual statements that do not pertain to human actions] the Qur’an says: The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the skeptics (3:60). Another verse is:

Rather, it is because all rational laws are deduced from external reality, which is nothing but God’s action and behavior. He is not a follower, but a leader and source of all rational principles. This can be confirmed by the numerous verses which urge the people to think, remember, contemplate, and investigate about God’s actions [that is, the world of creation]. As we said before, there are countless narrations through both Shia and Sunni chains of transmission about the types of Satan’s temptations and the variety of ways by which he makes different sins appealing to people. It is more than clear that the descriptions mentioned in these narrations are all symbolic representations that match various sins in terms of their quality and form. They are like the images that one sees in a dream according to one’s circumstances and beliefs. If we reflect on the second type of narrations quoted above [from number 25 to 29, which provide some explanation for what is meant by Satan’s acts], we can infer that narrations of the first type [from number

should emphasize is that all these are imaginal embodiments (tajassumāt mithāliyyah)2 that represent a certain act or thing, not a physical embodiment, as thought by the literalists (ḥashwiyyah) and some scholars of

hadith. For instance, they would interpret the above narration as follows: “While majūsiyyah (dualism, paganism) is a belief system among

humans, it is at the same time a leather belt that Satan wears.” They would also conclude that Satan really transforms into other beings with all their faculties, and becomes a member of that species—sometimes a human, sometimes an animal, and sometimes an inanimate object. Alternatively, they would say that Iblīs to these species is like matter (māddah) to form (ṣurah), where matter can assume different forms [and thus be actualized as a different species]. There are numerous narrations in this regard, which proves their authenticity as a group, but not individually. Likewise, the Qur’an confirms their overall idea, which is that Satan appears to our senses in various forms. This is what we can say about these narrations collectively. As

with each narration individually, it should first be authenticated. Even if it is found to have an authentic chain of narration—which is not the case about all of them—then it would be a solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid), and we cannot rely on solitary reports to infer our beliefs and roots of religion. At most it can be used in Islamic law, where a jurist may infer from it that a certain act is either mustaḥabb (recommended) or makrūh (reprehensible, disapproved).
